example: How much of the strip makes the three sides?
The joining tab overlaps; it is not a fourth side of the triangular stand.
exit: A revised stand uses two 3 1/4-in faces, a 4-in base and a 1/2-in joining tab. Find its blank length. Explain where you would measure the second fold from datum A. Cite your notebook and one test result.
key: Blank = 3 1/4 + 3 1/4 + 4 + 1/2 = 11 in. Second fold is 6 1/2 in from datum A. Actual tests vary; inspect independent tape use and a real revision, not only the digital answer.
title: Build a Stand for an Instruction Card
product: Make one triangular stand for a 3 × 5-in card, then improve its card-supporting lip. The 5-in card edge rests horizontally on the 4-in-wide stand.
why: A technician must turn a flat pattern into a useful object. Today you will read a cut/fold plan, measure fractions from one datum and check whether the product works.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two folder-card rectangles at least 10 1/2 × 4 in, one 4 × 1-in lip blank, one 4 × 1 1/2-in replacement lip blank, one paper/card rectangle 3 × 5 in, and 24 in of tape. Keep unused stock for a remake.
read: Drawing A labels the flat panels F (front), R (rear), B (base), T (joining tab) and L (separate lip). Solid outside lines are cut edges; dashed lines are folds. The finished side view shows B flat on the table.
measure: Cut the test card to 3 × 5 in. Mark its 5-in edge BOTTOM. The load today is this card.
On the body stock, choose the left 4-in edge as datum A. Mark 0, 3, 6, 10 and 10 1/2 in along BOTH long edges, always measuring from A.
Join matching marks with straight lines. Check overall width 4 in and length 10 1/2 in with your partner; then swap who reads the tape.
plan: Label F between 0–3 in, R between 3–6, B between 6–10, and T between 10–10 1/2. Do not cut the three inside lines.
Sketch the finished triangular side view in your notebook: two 3-in sloping faces and a 4-in base. Add the 1/2-in overlap tab on a separate detail.
build: Cut the OUTSIDE of the 10 1/2 × 4-in blank. Write your crew name on B.
Fold at 3, 6 and 10 in, all toward the same side of the card. Press the creases against a ruler; do not cut or score with a blade.
Place B flat on the desk. Bring the free edge of F to the fold between B and T. The 3-in faces meet at the top; the cross-section is a triangle.
Put T inside F, overlapping it by 1/2 in. Tape the seam across the full 4-in width. The tab is a joint, not a fourth side.
Cut L to 4 × 1 in. Draw and fold a line along its length, making two 4 × 1/2-in halves.

Tape one half of L to F at the bottom of the front face, with the lip fold at the front/base corner. Leave the other half projecting forward as a shelf; adjust that shelf approximately level with the tabletop.
Rest the card’s BOTTOM edge on L and lean the card back against F. Center it: about 1/2 in of card extends beyond each side of the stand.

Run the first three-trial test. Then cut a second lip 4 × 1 1/2 in; fold 1/2 in from one long edge. Replace L, attaching the 1/2-in half to F so the shelf is now 1 in deep. Label the new lip revision B.
Repeat the identical test. Keep the better lip on the stand; retain the removed lip with your notebook. If the body failed, remake it to the original dimensions before comparing lips.
test: Trial: put the stand on a level desk, place the card, remove both hands and time 10 seconds. Pass only if both stand and card stay upright. Remove the card; repeat for three trials.
Do three trials for the 1/2-in lip, then three for the 1-in lip. Record each pass/fail; a tie is a valid result.
Measure F and B along their fold-to-fold edges. Classroom layout check: 3 in and 4 in, each within ±1/8 in. Correct a wrong fold even if the card happens to stand.
done: One labeled triangular stand with a 3 × 5-in card; the spare lip beside it.
Notebook: labeled side view, actual F/B lengths, and a two-row table: lip depth | trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3. Save the individual transfer answer in the app.
prep: Set out seven kits, 15 notebooks and seven printed A sheets. Prebuild one finished sample and one unfolded labeled blank. Use 10 1/2-in stock, not a 10-in strip. A normal opened folder supplies the length.
demo: Say: “We are making THIS card stand. The 4-in panel goes on the table.” Show the completed sample before the flat plan. Model one mark from datum A, form the triangular loop, then show where T overlaps F and where L attaches. Release cutting only after both long edges have matching fold marks.
look: At minute 25 inspect 3/6/10-in marks. At minute 40 each student points to F/R/B/T on the blank. By minute 70 expect a standing triangle; by 95 expect six recorded trials. Ask each student to show the zero reference and read one fraction without a partner.
trouble: Four-sided loop → T was treated as a panel; overlap it inside F. Card slides → shelf must project below the card, not be taped flat against F. Stand rocks → straighten the seam and check B is the 4-in panel. No apparent improvement → record the tie; do not invent a failure.

example: Find the interior and outside width of three clear bays.
3 × 2 1/2 + 2 × 1/8 = 7 3/4 in interior; + 2 × 1/8 = 8 in outside.
Only the two internal partitions belong in the interior-width sum.
exit: Two clear bays each need 3 1/4 in. One internal partition is 1/8 in and two outer walls are each 1/8 in. Calculate outside width and identify the internal partition on your sketch.
key: Outside width = 6 1/2 + 3/8 = 6 7/8 in. Interior width = 6 5/8 in. Check that the student adds three thicknesses for the outside width, not two.
title: Mock Up a Three-Bay Supply Tray
product: Build a folder-card tray with three side-by-side bays for erasers, binder clips and paper clips. Keep this version for comparison.
why: Storage fit depends on inside clearance, not just outside size. This prototype gives us a real fit problem to measure before using stronger material.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Folder card for the seven parts in drawing B; two erasers, three binder clips and six paper clips; 36 in of tape. B = base 8 × 6 in; F and R = two long walls 8 × 2 in; E1, E2, D1 and D2 = four short-wall blanks 6 × 2 in. Trim short walls to the measured gap between F and R.
read: B shows a top view and assembly. F/R run the full 8-in width. E1/E2 fit BETWEEN them. D1/D2 run front-to-back. The 1/8-in thickness and 2 1/2-in clear bays on the example are supplied math values; measure the actual folder version.
measure: Measure the three types of supplies at their widest point. Make a table: item | width | unit.
Mark the base 8 × 6 in. From its left edge, mark lines at 2 5/8 and 5 1/4 in across the base; these locate the LEFT faces of D1 and D2.
plan: Draw an 8 × 6-in top view. Label the front edge F and the left outer edge datum A.
Copy the seven-part list. Assign left bay = erasers, middle = binder clips, right = paper clips. This is the required first arrangement.
build: Cut B, F and R to their labeled sizes. Cut E1/E2/D1/D2 initially as 6 × 2-in rectangles.
Stand F and R on TOP of B, with their outside faces flush to its front and rear edges. Tape each wall to B inside and outside; keep walls upright.
Set E1 between F and R at the left edge. Mark the actual inside gap on E1; trim to that mark so it fits without bending F/R. Use it to mark the other three short walls, then check each fit.
Tape E1/E2 upright with outside faces flush to the left/right edges of B.
Tape D1/D2 upright with their LEFT faces on the two base lines. Tape both ends to F/R and bottom edges to B.
Put the assigned supplies in their bays. Partner removes and returns each type three times while the tray stays on the desk.
Circle one snag on your notebook top view. Write one specific proposed repair: loose joint → reinforce; object catches divider → move that divider 1/4 in. Keep the prototype intact for day 3.
test: Each type fits its assigned bay and can be removed without lifting the tray. Record three attempts for each type.
Measure each clear bay between wall faces at the front and rear. Record the six readings, even if they are unequal.
done: One three-bay folder tray with seven labeled parts and the supplies in it.
Notebook: top view, six clearance readings, retrieval results and one circled problem.
prep: Provide ordinary folder stock and identical test supplies in all seven kits. Cut a sample short wall to show fitting between F/R. Do not substitute a free-choice organizer brief.
demo: Show why a 6-in short-wall blank must be trimmed when long walls occupy part of the 6-in base. Demonstrate dry fitting, marking and trimming one end. Point to “outside” and “clear” on the real tray.
look: Check F/R sit on the base, partitions run front-to-back, and all students can identify the same datum. Accept small unequal bays for thin stock; the 2 1/2-in example assumes 1/8-in stock.
trouble: Walls bow → the short pieces are too long; dry-fit and trim. Bay narrows toward rear → divider is angled; retape square to F. Supplies snag → mark the actual contact, not a vague “bad fit.”

example: Can four rectangular pieces fit this sheet?
Each 4 × 3-in piece has 12 in² area; four use 48 in². Two rows of two fit in an 8 × 6-in rectangle.
A 9 × 12-in sheet can contain this arrangement. Area alone would not prove a different set of shapes fits.
exit: A 12 × 9-in sheet supplies six 4 × 3-in pieces. Show an arrangement, calculate used area and remaining area, and explain why the layout matters.
key: Three columns of 4 in and two rows of 3 in fit: 12 × 6 in. Used area 72 in²; sheet 108 in²; remaining 36 in². An equivalent rotated layout is acceptable.
title: Measure and Cut the Durable Tray Parts
product: Make the seven fitted parts for a stronger copy of the same three-bay tray; dry-fit them before assembly.
why: Fabricators use a cut list to avoid wasting stock. You will transfer dimensions and account for the actual wall thickness.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Previous prototype, clean thin packaging card totaling at least 130 in² of usable area per crew, and 12 in of temporary tape. B = base 8 × 6 in; F and R = two long walls 8 × 2 in; E1, E2, D1 and D2 = four short-wall blanks 6 × 2 in. Trim short walls to the measured gap between F and R.
read: Use B’s part labels and top/front views. Height is 2 in above the base; depth is 6 in front-to-back. A wall blank’s length is not the same as the finished inside gap.
measure: Measure usable stock. Lay out 8 × 6 base, two 8 × 2 walls and four 6 × 2 blanks; each student marks at least one part.
Mark D1/D2 positions at 2 5/8 and 5 1/4 in from the base’s left edge. Check both endpoints before drawing each line.
plan: Make a cut-list table: part | quantity | blank length | height/depth | final fitted length. Enter B×1, F/R×2, E/D×4.
Draw the rectangles on available stock with no overlaps. Shared scissors cuts need no added saw kerf. Preserve long straight offcuts.
build: Cut B, F and R first. Label each part on the face that will be outside.
Temporarily tape F/R upright on B with outer faces flush to the base edges.
Use a narrow scrap strip to capture the inside gap: hold one end against F, mark where it meets the inside face of R, then measure that length.
Transfer that gap to all four short-wall blanks. Mark a waste X on the portion to remove.
Partner checks the first marked short wall; trim it and test it between F/R without bending either wall.
Trim the remaining three to the same checked length. Label E1/E2/D1/D2.
Dry-fit all seven pieces in their specified positions. Do not permanently tape partitions today. Bundle small parts in the base with the cut list.
test: Each short wall fits between F/R without force and with no end gap greater than 1/8 in.
Check one 8-in part and one fitted part independently. Record intended, actual and signed difference; ±1/8 in is the classroom cutting tolerance.
done: Seven labeled durable parts that dry-fit the tray plan.
Notebook: stock layout, complete final cut list and two inspection readings per student.
prep: Collect seven sets of thin, clean packaging card that scissors can cut. Adult-precut thick corrugated material; do not introduce utility knives to this lesson. Supply two spare short-wall blanks per crew.
demo: Model measuring the actual inside gap with a story strip. Compare the physical gap with the example 6 − 2(1/8) = 5 3/4 in. Explain that their fitted length comes from their own stock.
look: Inspect one cut per student before the rest are cut. The list must name which parts share the same fitted length; students may not silently use 6 in for all four.
trouble: Too short → replace that part using a spare; tape cannot restore a missing wall length accurately. Too long → mark and trim only the excess. Stock too thick for scissors → teacher substitutes thinner card or supplies precut blanks.

example: Estimate the cost using classroom prices, not a supplier quote.
This is material consumed. Buying one whole sheet would cost $2.40 before tape or other supplies.
exit: Your build consumes 3/4 sheet at a classroom price of $2.40 per sheet and 4 ft of tape at $0.10/ft. Find consumed-material cost and the purchase cost if you must buy one sheet plus that tape.
key: Consumed cost = $1.80 + $0.40 = $2.20. Whole-sheet purchase = $2.40 + $0.40 = $2.80. Do not present sample prices as current quotations.
title: Assemble and Reinforce the Supply Tray
product: Assemble the durable tray and add four folded corner reinforcements; compare it with the folder prototype.
why: A stronger joint consumes material and time. You will make that change deliberately and calculate a transparent classroom material cost.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Seven durable parts from day 3, prototype, four 2 × 2-in card squares, the same test supplies, and a measured 48-in tape allowance.
read: Use B’s assembly labels. The four extra squares become angle brackets: one vertical center fold makes two 1 × 2-in legs; each leg attaches to a different wall at an inside corner.
measure: Measure and mark the four 2 × 2-in squares and their 1-in center folds.
Record starting tape allowance 48 in; measure unused tape at the end. Use the final cut-list dimensions, not the raw blank sizes, for area.
plan: Copy revision B onto the top view and mark the four reinforced outside corners.
Set up a material table: card area (in²), tape used (in), tape used ÷ 12 (ft). The worked example uses supplied classroom prices, not actual store prices.
build: Tape F/R to B, then fit and tape E1/E2 using the checked part lengths.
Put D1/D2 left faces on their marked lines; tape bottoms and ends.
Fold each reinforcing square 90 degrees along its centerline.
Fit one bracket vertically inside each outer corner. Tape one leg to the long wall and one to the end wall; leave the bottom against B.
Move the same supplies from the prototype into the same labeled bays.
Run the retrieval test on both versions. If a reinforced corner catches an object, trim only the projecting tape and retest.
Measure remaining tape and calculate used length. Label the durable tray revision B and retain prototype A.
test: For each version, remove/return each supply type three times. Count snags and loose joints using the same operator and objects.
Measure outside width and one clear bay. Check that reinforcement did not block the assigned objects.
done: An assembled durable three-bay tray with four angle brackets; prototype retained.
Notebook: before/after retrieval table, finished dimensions and actual tape-use calculation.
prep: Have seven 48-in tape strips on backing sheets plus replacement stock for failed joints. State that the tape allowance is a measurement budget, not a reason to leave a needed repair unsafe or incomplete.
demo: Show a flat square becoming an inside-corner bracket. Demonstrate that the two legs join two different walls. Calculate one sample area and convert 24 in of tape to 2 ft.
look: Look for real corner brackets, unchanged test objects, and a measured tape remainder. Both students must name a changed joint and explain the purpose.
trouble: Bracket blocks a bay → flatten it tightly against the corner; remove protruding tape. Tray still flexes → check the wall-to-base seam before adding decorative layers. Cost differs from example → use their measured quantity and the explicitly supplied price.

example: Check an inspected dimension.
Actual 8 1/8 in − intended 8 in = +1/8 in.
A teacher-set ±1/8-in tolerance includes both limits; whether this is suitable depends on the object and material.
exit: A plan calls for 6 3/4 in ±1/8 in. State the acceptable interval. Does an actual 6 7/8-in part meet it? Give your own final measurement and notebook reference.
key: Interval 6 5/8 through 6 7/8 in, inclusive. 6 7/8 in meets the stated dimensional tolerance. It still needs the functional fit test.
title: Inspect and Hand Over the Finished Tray
product: Deliver the three-bay tray, a matching top/front drawing and a completed fit inspection.
why: A customer needs a working product and a drawing that matches it. An inspector must separate dimensional tolerance from functional fit.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Both tray versions, original test supplies, final cut list and one blank inspection page.
read: Read B’s top view for width/depth/partition locations; read its front view for wall height. Update your own drawing to match the actual revision.
measure: Individually measure outside width, depth and one clear bay. Record intended | actual | difference | pass/rework.
Use outside width 8 in ±1/8 and depth 6 in ±1/8 as classroom checks. Clear-bay fit is checked with its assigned object.
plan: Draw the final top and front views with units, datum, actual partition positions and revision B.
Write this three-line handover: what goes in each bay; how to move the tray (support the base); which joint was improved.
build: Exchange tray and drawings with another crew. Inspect without changing their work.
Identify one mismatch between drawing and object; if none is found, record “no mismatch found” and the dimensions checked.
Return the tray. Its owners correct the marked drawing or refit the inaccurate part, then repeat the affected measurement.
Run the nine retrieval attempts with the original supplies.
Give the receiving crew a 60-second handover using the object and drawing.
Each student shows the teacher one tape reading and traces one part from plan to object. Store both versions in the labeled tray.
test: All three supply types fit and can be retrieved without lifting the tray; note each failure.
Drawing and product agree within the stated checks. A dimensional pass does not excuse a failed retrieval.
done: A handed-over working tray, two-view drawing and honest inspection record.
Each student completes the app transfer answer and a live tape/plan check.
prep: Pair crews for exchange and prepare a roster with three separate columns: math, measuring, plan reading. Spend the make interval circulating for short individual checks.
demo: Model a signed error: 8 1/8 − 8 = +1/8 in. Show where the top and front views describe the same wall. Model one concise handover.
look: Record independent / with cue / not observed separately. Require the student to place the tape and read it; do not accept the partner’s number as an individual check.
trouble: Drawing differs from a sound product → revise the drawing and label the revision. A required item still snags → fix the contact point, then repeat all three attempts for that item.

example: Find the center spacing.
Horizontal: 8 1/2 − 2 × 3/4 = 7 in. Vertical: 5 1/4 − 2 × 3/4 = 3 3/4 in.
Overall dimensions and center spacing are different quantities.
exit: If both horizontal edge offsets become 1 in while overall width stays 8 1/2 in, what is the new center spacing? Which two marks move?
key: Spacing = 6 1/2 in. Both left and right columns of centers move inward by 1/4 in; all four centers change horizontal position.
title: Clinic: Make a Four-Center Mounting Template
product: Individually make a paper mounting template with four located centers; use the skill to inspect the tray.
why: Installers locate holes from edges and centers. The paper template lets you practice that skill without drilling.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. One 8 1/2 × 5 1/4-in paper rectangle per student, one spare sheet and the completed tray.
read: C gives four center marks 3/4 in from their two nearest edges. Mark centers only; do not cut holes.
measure: Choose lower-left as (0,0). Mark x = 3/4 and 7 3/4 in along bottom and top.
Mark y = 3/4 and 4 1/2 in along left and right. Draw light crossing guide lines.
plan: Copy a center table: left-bottom (3/4,3/4), right-bottom (7 3/4,3/4), left-top (3/4,4 1/2), right-top (7 3/4,4 1/2), all in inches.
Calculate the horizontal and vertical center spacing before marking the centers.
build: Lay out the rectangle independently. Cut its outside edge only.
Use the four guide-line intersections to draw four small crosses.
Exchange templates; checker measures offsets from the named datum without correcting marks.
Mark an inaccurate cross with a small circle, then make the corrected cross beside it. Keep the first attempt visible.
Draw revision B with horizontal offsets of 1 in from each side; keep vertical offsets 3/4 in.
Return to the tray and independently check one partition’s position from its left outside edge. Correct its drawing if needed.
test: All four original centers are within ±1/16 in of their specified positions.
Revision B horizontal spacing is checked separately; retain both versions.
done: Two individually marked paper templates and one tray position check.
Notebook includes coordinates, spacing calculation and any correction.
prep: This is the defined flex lesson when extra practice is needed. Print C and provide larger fraction strips for students who need them; all still make their own final template.
demo: Demonstrate one center with two edge offsets. Show that a center is the intersection of two locations, not the corner of a drawn box.
look: Ask students to read 7 3/4 on the tape and distinguish overall width from center spacing. Each student keeps their own sheet.
trouble: Offsets measured from different unmarked ends → relabel datum and remeasure. Crosses correct but spacing wrong → measure center-to-center, not from a paper edge.

example: Compare improvement against a baseline.
Version 1 holds 4 identical objects; version 2 holds 7: (7 − 4)/4 × 100 = 75% more.
Object count is a comparative load measure, not force in newtons. A capped test gives a lower bound on capacity.
exit: A tower improves from 5 to 8 identical test objects. Find percent increase. Read the footprint limit from drawing D and explain why taller is not automatically stronger.
key: 60% increase. Footprint limit is 6 × 6 in. Strength depends on geometry, material, load path and stability; height alone is not evidence.
title: Build and Load-Test Two Paper Towers
product: Build two 11-in paper columns supporting a 6 × 6-in platform; add base ties and repeat the same capped load test.
why: Builders need a continuous load path and stable supports. A capped test shows what the model carried under specified conditions.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two letter sheets for two 6 1/2 × 11-in column blanks, two 6 × 1-in offcut ties, one 6 × 6-in card platform, one small paper cup, ten identical large paper clips and 36 in of tape.
read: D shows two triangular columns. Each blank folds at 2, 4 and 6 in across its 6 1/2-in width; its full 11-in length is the height. The final 1/2 in is an overlap.
measure: Mark both blanks from the same long edge at 2/4/6 in; measure height 11 in.
Draw a 6 × 6-in footprint on scrap. Keep both columns and platform inside it.
plan: Sketch the side and top views; show the two triangular column footprints under the left/right sides of the platform.
Prepare a load table with rows 0 through 10 clips for version A and B. The cup/platform are the same in both tests.
build: Cut, fold and tape each blank into a triangular tube with three 2-in faces. Keep both ends level.
Stand the columns on the marked footprint, one under each side of the platform. Place the 6 × 6-in platform across them; tape its contacts lightly.
Put the empty cup at the platform center. If it cannot support the cup, repair the column seams before recording a load trial.
Add one paper clip every five seconds up to ten. Stop immediately if a column tips, folds or the platform falls; do not catch a falling load with the model.
Unload. Cut two 6 × 1-in ties from offcuts. Tape one tie across the front column bases and one across the rear bases to resist spreading; do not tape the tower to the table.
Repeat the same 0–10-clip test with the same cup, platform and placement. Record the cap if both versions hold ten.
test: Freestanding footprint no larger than 6 × 6 in; height 11 in ±1/4.
Record last load held for five seconds and failure location. Ten clips means “held the test cap,” not “maximum strength is ten.”
done: One tower with two triangular columns and removable base ties.
Two load records and an annotated load-path sketch.
prep: Prebuild one sample using the actual paper. Use large paper clips as identical low-mass loads; count rather than infer newtons. Test at tabletop height with the area clear of faces.
demo: Show the 1/2-in column overlap and level ends. Trace load from cup to platform, columns and tabletop. Explain when to stop and how to record a capped result.
look: All crews use two equal blanks and identical loading increments. Check ties connect column bases, not the tabletop.
trouble: Top tilts before loading → unequal column ends; square the ends or remake. Both reach cap → report the tie; the next lesson tests shape under a different loading condition.

example: Calculate bearing from actual geometry.
A centered 11-in member over an 8-in gap has (11 − 8)/2 = 1 1/2 in bearing at each end.
The clear gap excludes the supports; total member length includes both bearings.
exit: A beam spans 9 1/4 in with 3/4 in bearing at each end. What minimum length is needed? Sketch where the three lengths sit.
key: 10 3/4 in. The three consecutive segments are bearing, clear gap, bearing. Material results depend on observed data.
title: Compare Flat, V and Channel Beams
product: Make three equal-paper beams and compare midpoint deflection over the same 8-in gap.
why: Cross-section changes stiffness without necessarily changing material quantity. You will measure that effect before choosing structural shapes.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Three 10 × 3-in paper strips, two equal-height book stacks, one small paper cup with five large paper clips, and a vertical ruler.
read: D2 labels an 8-in CLEAR span with 1 in bearing at each end. Sample A is flat; B has one lengthwise center fold (V); C has lengthwise folds 1 in from each edge (channel).
measure: Set inside faces of the book stacks exactly 8 in apart. Mark the strip ends at 1 and 9 in.
Measure the midpoint height relative to the tabletop, first empty and then loaded; use the same point on the beam.
plan: Sketch the three end-on cross-sections and label equal blank area 10 × 3 = 30 in².
Make table: shape | unloaded height mm | loaded height mm | deflection mm | collapsed?
build: Leave A flat. Fold B lengthwise at 1 1/2 in to make an open V. Fold C at 1 and 2 in to make a U-channel with a 1-in floor and upright sides.
Place A with 1 in resting on each support. Mark its midpoint at 5 in from an end.
Measure unloaded midpoint height. Place the same cup with five clips at the midpoint, release and measure after five seconds.
Remove the load and repeat with B, ridge down so the cup bridges its upper edges, then C, channel opening up.
Repeat the three tests once. If a beam collapses, record collapse instead of inventing a deflection.
Make a second copy of the least-deflecting shape. Recheck its span and loading to see whether the result repeats.
test: All blanks have equal area and use the same span, bearing, cup and clip load.
Report two trials per shape. Do not call a collapsed specimen “zero deflection.”
done: Three labeled beam shapes and one repeated sample.
Notebook cross-sections and six test rows.
prep: Use identical book heights and the same cup/load at all stations. Precheck that midpoint can be observed beside the cup. Have spare paper for collapsed specimens.
demo: Show clear span versus total length using the support faces. Demonstrate loaded and unloaded readings from one fixed tabletop reference.
look: Measure one student’s 8-in gap and observe how they subtract heights. A bending result is not proof of compression-column strength.
trouble: Cup rolls or tips → center it and use the same broad-base paper cup for every shape. Beam slides → align bearing marks; do not silently add tape supports to only one sample.

example: Convert feet and inches consistently.
6 in is half a foot, not 0.6 ft.
exit: Convert a 9 ft 8-in surveyed length to inches. On drawing E, how far from the southwest corner is the far edge of the 3-ft door?
key: 116 in. Door far edge is 2 + 3 = 5 ft from the specified corner along the south wall.
title: Survey a Doorway and Lay Out the Community Room
product: Measure a real doorway, then make the supplied community-room floor plan. Keep the two sets of dimensions separate.
why: Surveyors record existing conditions; designers read proposed conditions. Mixing them can put an opening in the wrong place.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two sheets of paper and access to one teacher-designated classroom wall/doorway; two 1 × 2-in card table tokens and one 1/2 × 1/2-in person token.
read: E is the required fictional community room: 16 × 12 ft; south door begins 2 ft from southwest corner and is 3 ft wide. Survey measurements do not replace E’s dimensions.
measure: At the designated doorway, identify the classroom-side left wall corner as survey datum. Measure corner-to-near-jamb and opening width to nearest 1/4 in.
Measure twice, with roles swapped. Record both readings in feet/inches AND total inches. Keep the passage clear.
plan: Title one sketch EXISTING DOOR SURVEY and show the datum and two actual measurements.
On a second sheet draw the PROPOSED ROOM at 1/2 in = 1 ft: 8 × 6 in, north at top, door opening along bottom from x=1 to 2 1/2 in.
build: Mark the model floor rectangle and door jambs from the southwest datum.
Cut two 1 × 2-in table tokens and label them 2 × 4-ft tables.
Put both tables against the north edge, with their 2-in sides east-west. Leave 1 in between them.
Cut a 1/2-in square person token. Move it from the south entrance to each table without crossing a table.
Trace a clear route on the floor plan. If blocked, move only the eastern table toward the east wall and repeat.
Attach tokens with small tape loops so they remain movable. Store the floor plan for the next lesson.
test: A partner locates the surveyed opening from written dimensions alone.
The proposed plan remains exactly 8 × 6 in with the specified door position. The token can reach both tables; this is a model-use test, not an accessibility certification.
done: One measured survey sketch and one proposed floor layout with two table tokens and a clear route.
Notebook labels distinguish measured school values from supplied design values.
prep: Name the actual survey door before class. Put a small removable datum label at the agreed classroom corner. Assign crews staggered survey turns while others begin the proposed layout.
demo: Measure one door width and convert feet/inches to total inches. Then point to E and say: “This separate design stays 16 by 12 feet, regardless of our survey.”
look: Check students have two clearly titled drawings and record repeat readings, not an unexplained averaged guess.
trouble: Feet written as decimal inches → model 9 ft 8 in = 116 in. Proposed doorway copied from real room → restore the supplied design and retain survey on its separate page.

example: Transfer real dimensions to the model.
16 ft × 1/2 in/ft = 8 in; 12 ft × 1/2 in/ft = 6 in; 3-ft door = 1 1/2 in.
Both plan and elevation must use the same chosen model scale.
exit: A 14-ft wall with an 8-ft height uses the model scale 1/2 in = 1 ft. Find model width and height. Explain what changes if a printed drawing is resized.
key: 7 × 4 in. Resizing changes the measurable paper scale; written dimensions remain the stated values. Verify a calibration dimension before scaling from paper.
title: Build the Scale Room and Working Door
product: Make the 8 × 6-in community-room shell with 4-in walls, a hinged south door and movable table tokens.
why: A coordinated plan and elevation must describe the same opening. You will transfer real dimensions to a physical model.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Thin folder/card stock for the five room parts, previous floor layout/tokens, 48 in tape. Base 8 × 6 in; N/S walls 8 × 4 in; E/W blanks 6 × 4 in (trim to fit between N/S); roof 8 × 6 in. South door: left jamb 1 in from west end, opening 1 1/2 in wide × 3 1/2 in high. Roof is made on day 6.
read: E shows floor plan and south elevation. A 3 × 7-ft door becomes 1 1/2 × 3 1/2 in. West jamb is 1 in from the model southwest corner in both views.
measure: Mark base 8 × 6 in and N/S walls 8 × 4 in. Mark E/W blanks 6 × 4 in.
On S mark door jambs at x=1 and 2 1/2 in, and lintel 3 1/2 in above the bottom edge.
plan: Draw south elevation 8 × 4 in with the same door dimensions. Label all model dimensions in inches and write the full-size scale.
Copy the five-part cut list and label outside faces N/S/E/W.
build: Cut base and four walls. On S cut the right jamb and top of the door; fold along the left jamb to leave a hinged door flap. The bottom edge is already free.
Tape N and S upright on top of the base with outer faces flush to the base edges; keep the door free of tape.
Dry-fit E/W BETWEEN N/S. Mark the actual inside gap and trim their width so the shell closes without bowing.
Tape E/W to base and adjoining walls. Use small inside and outside tape pieces at each joint.
Label north and datum SW on the base. Return the two table tokens to their recorded positions.
Swing the door inward at least 90 degrees. Move the person token from entrance to each table.
Adjust only table positions if they block the door/route; update their positions on the plan.
test: Base is 8 × 6 in and wall height 4 in, each within ±1/8 in. Door opening dimensions and offset are within ±1/16 in.
Door opens 90 degrees without touching furniture; top and front drawings agree with actual door location.
done: A four-wall room model with working hinged south door and two tables; no roof yet.
Coordinated top/front drawings and at least four model scale conversions.
prep: Precut thick card if required; thin folder stock permits student scissors. Show one completed shell and the door’s two cut edges/one fold edge.
demo: Demonstrate the conversion and point to the same left jamb in plan, elevation and physical wall. Cut only top and right of the door; a loose rectangle is not the intended hinge.
look: Check two conversions independently before cutting. At assembly inspect E/W dry-fit and datum consistency.
trouble: Door cut off → reattach left edge with a tape hinge and record repair. Wrong corner used → relabel outside face before trimming. Door rubs base → trim a very small bottom sliver and record the clearance.

example: Find a diagonal for a right-angled frame.
For a 6 × 8-in rectangle: d² = 6² + 8² = 100; d = 10 in.
This uses a right angle. Check the frame; do not apply it to an arbitrary four-sided shape.
exit: A right-angled bay is 3 × 4 in. Calculate its diagonal. Identify which view would show a brace on a vertical wall.
key: 5 in by the Pythagorean relationship. The wall elevation shows the vertical-wall brace; the floor plan alone does not show its height.
title: Test a Wall Frame and Add a Diagonal
product: Build a separate 6 × 8-in joint-center frame, test its racking and add a diagonal brace; then reinforce the model room’s corners.
why: A diagonal changes how a rectangular frame resists shape change. You will connect a measured test with a bracing decision.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two 9 × 1-in and two 7 × 1-in card strips, one 11 × 1-in brace, four 2 × 2-in corner squares, string, cup with ten large paper clips, two books and the model room.
read: E2 dimensions run BETWEEN joint centers: 8 in horizontal and 6 in vertical. Each strip extends 1/2 in past each joint center; diagonal center spacing is 10 in.
measure: Mark each strip centerline and points 1/2 in from its ends. Mark brace attachment centers 1/2 and 10 1/2 in from one end.
Measure both frame diagonals between joint centers before the test; a square 6 × 8-in rectangle has two 10-in diagonals.
plan: Sketch the four joint centers as a 6 × 8-in rectangle. Draw the brace from bottom-left to top-right.
Make table: unbraced / braced | starting top-right height | loaded height | downward movement, in mm.
build: Arrange the two long strips horizontally and short strips vertically with center marks overlapping. Tape each overlap on both faces; keep joints flexible enough to rack.
Stand the frame vertical. Sandwich its left upright between two upright books and tape it to the outer book face so both left joint centers stay fixed. Teacher checks the books are stable.
Tie the loaded cup to the TOP-RIGHT joint with a short string. Keep the cup close to the tabletop; no one holds the right side.
Measure the top-right joint height from the tabletop before loading and after five seconds of load. Remove the cup.
Return the frame to its original rectangular shape. Tape the diagonal between bottom-left and top-right centers; use the 11-in strip’s 1/2-in end allowances.
Repeat with the identical cup/clip load and fixed left side.
Fold each 2 × 2-in square into an angle bracket. Tape one inside each corner of the model room without blocking its door; label this model revision B.
test: Compare vertical movement at the same joint under the same load. Report any movement too small to resolve with the ruler.
Check the brace joins opposite joint centers and the room door still swings 90 degrees.
done: A braced test frame and four reinforced corners on the room model.
Two diagonals and before/after racking data with a labeled frame sketch.
prep: Set up and rehearse the book fixture with the actual card. Use ten paper clips in the same cup for both tests, not an unspecified hand push. Stabilize book bases with another flat book if needed.
demo: Show the difference between a 9-in strip and its 8-in joint spacing. Hang the cup from the same top-right point twice; demonstrate how the ruler reads vertical movement.
look: Check the 6/8/10 triangle arithmetic and observe that the left side remains fixed. A small or tied result is acceptable; it is not full-size structural validation.
trouble: Whole fixture moves → stabilize books and repeat; that trial is invalid. Brace loose → tape at the center marks. Frame collapses → unload and repair; record failure instead of a fictitious displacement.

example: Estimate net covering area.
A 12 × 8-ft wall minus a 3 × 7-ft opening: 96 − 21 = 75 ft². With a stated 10% allowance: 82.5 ft².
Allowance is a planning choice, not a universal trade rule; purchase quantities depend on usable stock sizes.
exit: A 10 × 8-ft wall has a 2 × 3-ft opening. Find net area and area with a supplied 10% allowance. Identify the opening in the elevation.
key: 80 − 6 = 74 ft²; 74 × 1.10 = 81.4 ft². Do not subtract the opening perimeter from wall area.
title: Close the Room and Count the Material
product: Make a removable roof and a materials takeoff for the model’s walls, door opening and roof.
why: Estimators subtract openings and distinguish surface area from purchased sheet quantities. A removable roof lets the next worker inspect the interior.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Model room, one 8 × 6-in card roof, two 2 × 1-in card locator strips and 12 in tape.
read: E supplies nominal outside dimensions. Roof is 8 × 6 in. The south wall’s door area is 1 1/2 × 3 1/2 in; keep the hinged door even though the opening is excluded from wall-covering area.
measure: Measure the actual outside roof-bearing rectangle and compare with 8 × 6 in.
Measure door opening, not the flap including any overlap. Record the model’s actual dimensions separately from nominal takeoff values.
plan: Calculate nominal wall area: two 8 × 4 plus two 6 × 4; subtract door area once. Add 8 × 6 roof separately.
Draw the roof underside with two locator tabs near the north/south edges. These keep the roof from sliding; it stays lift-off.
build: Cut roof 8 × 6 in. Mark underside and north edge.
Fold each 2 × 1-in strip at its midpoint to make an L with 1-in legs.
Place roof upside down. Tape one leg of a tab near the center of its north edge; locate the fold just inside the actual north wall position.
Fit the roof. The free tab leg drops INSIDE the north wall. Mark and attach the second tab to fit inside the south wall.
Lift and replace the roof three times. Trim tab width or adjust its location if it catches a wall.
Write a small material label under the roof: nominal wall covering, roof area and actual card used.
test: Roof covers the wall tops and lifts off without pulling walls apart; repeat three times.
Takeoff subtracts the door once: wall covering 106 3/4 in²; roof 48 in². Treat overlaps and actual stock cutting waste separately.
done: One room model with removable located roof.
Notebook takeoff with units, door subtraction and a sketch of the tab detail.
prep: Prepare spare roof stock and a sample locator tab. The given model-area key is for nominal panels; actual end-wall trimming changes precise consumed area.
demo: Demonstrate net area by shading the door opening. Show a roof tab under the lid instead of taping the roof permanently shut.
look: Check students distinguish in from in² and roof from wall area. Ask each to point to the opening being subtracted.
trouble: Roof pulls wall inward → tabs too far inside; reposition. Door area counted twice → one opening in one wall. A sheet-area total alone does not prove the cut layout will fit.

example: Compare melting in a controlled test.
12 g melted from 60 g = 20%; 6 g from 60 g = 10%. Melt reduction = (12 − 6)/12 × 100 = 50%.
The enclosure halved melt in this trial; it did not establish a material R-value.
exit: A control melts 15 g and an insulated version melts 9 g in comparable trials. Find percent melt reduction. State one condition that must be held the same.
key: 40% reduction relative to control. Accept equal starting mass/temperature, duration, container, surroundings or handling. No R-value inference.
title: Build and Test an Insulated Cup Enclosure
product: Make a two-layer paper enclosure for one ice cup and compare it with an identical uninsulated control cup.
why: Envelope performance requires a fair comparison. You will keep starting ice, time and handling the same while changing the insulation.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two identical dry 240–250-mL plastic cups, two identical paper/card lids, two letter-paper sheets, tape, tray, timer, sieve, catch cup, 1-g balance and 120 g ice per crew (60 g for each cup). Shared balance station is acceptable.
read: F shows the same inner cup in control and insulated conditions. Both have identical flat lids; only the test cup gets the paper wrap and bottom pad.
measure: Measure cup circumference with a paper strip, marking one full wrap; measure cup height with ruler.
At the balance station tare each dry cup and add 60 g ice to each. Start both cups together.
plan: Draw a section: cup, two paper wrap layers and 1/2-in crumpled-paper bottom pad. Label the control’s matching lid.
Prepare table: cup | starting ice g | elapsed min | collected melt g | observations. Test interval is 20 min.
build: Cut two paper strips each cup-height tall and circumference + 1 in long. Tape them end-to-end if needed to reach that measured length.
Wrap the test cup twice, one strip at a time, loosely enough to leave small air spaces; tape only the seams. Keep paper dry and outside the cup.
Make a 1/2-in-thick lightly crumpled pad from remaining paper and place it under the test cup. Control sits directly on the same tray.
Add the equal ice masses, put matching lids on both and start a 20-minute timer. Keep them side-by-side away from sun/vents.
During the wait, make a 4 × 4-in two-layer wall sample for the model room and draw its layers; do not disturb cups.
At 20 minutes drain each cup through the same sieve into the tared catch cup for 30 seconds. Weigh the collected melt, drying/taring the catch cup between samples.
Calculate control melt minus insulated melt. Calculate percent reduction only if control melt is greater than zero; keep all readings even if insulation did worse.
test: Both start with 60 g ice, have the same lid and run for the same 20 minutes; record any deviation.
Readings at/below the 1-g instrument resolution are inconclusive. Do not replace them with the worked example or claim an R-value.
done: One insulated cup enclosure and one 4 × 4-in wall-layer sample.
Actual control/test melt results, a section sketch and a supported comparison.
prep: Collect matching cups, ice, a sieve and 1-g balance before release. Run one 20-minute preparation check to ensure melt is measurable in the room. If not, schedule a longer whole-class interval and print that single interval before class; do not improvise different times per crew.
demo: Demonstrate tare, equal starting mass and the 30-second drain. Explain that we weigh melt, not water plus cup, and that both cups receive identical lids.
look: Launch thermal tests early in Make so the 20-minute wait fits. Use the waiting interval for the wall sample. Check both times and all mass units.
trouble: Wet paper → note changed conditions and remake for a repeat. No measurable melt → report insufficient resolution; continue wall sample and arrange a longer repeat. Zero control melt → percentage is undefined.

example: Calculate the effect of a measured change.
Deflection falls from 6 mm to 4 mm: (6 − 4)/6 × 100 ≈ 33.3% reduction.
Report measurement resolution; a small difference may not be meaningful enough to justify a strong claim.
exit: Movement changes from 8 mm to 5 mm. Calculate the reduction and name the baseline. Identify the revised feature on the relevant drawing view.
key: 37.5% reduction using 8 mm as baseline. A claim of improvement needs comparable actual testing and instrument resolution.
title: Seal One Insulation Gap and Retest
product: Improve the insulated cup’s top-edge fit, repeat the comparison, and add a removable insulation panel to the room.
why: A redesign needs one identified change and comparable test conditions. You will change the top-edge seal while holding the rest of the test constant.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Previous cup enclosure and wall sample, fresh equal ice masses, identical control materials, same balance/test equipment, one 4 × 1-in paper strip and two tape loops.
read: F’s layer section now receives a paper collar around the test cup top. The matching control keeps the same original lid. This is a revision to the cup enclosure, not proof of whole-building performance.
measure: Measure the largest gap between insulation wrap and lid; record to the ruler’s nearest division.
Measure the north wall panel area to confirm the 4 × 4-in sample will fit without covering a door or roof locator.
plan: Draw revision C with the added collar. Keep the original section visible; circle only the new piece.
Copy original melt values and conditions into a before/after table. Each new run also needs its own control cup.
build: Dry the enclosure completely. Replace damaged paper with the same number of layers.
Make a 1-in-high collar of paper, length = measured cup circumference + 1 in; join strips if required. Fit it around the top of the wrap to bridge the lid-edge gap; do not add layers elsewhere.
Repeat the equal-ice, matching-control test for the same agreed interval and 30-second drainage used on day 7.
During the wait, attach the 4 × 4-in wall sample inside the north wall using two removable tape loops.
Lift the roof, remove/replace the panel and swing the door 90 degrees. Adjust loops if access is blocked.
Compare each insulated result with its own control. If melt is greater after revision, keep the data and write that the change did not improve this trial.
test: One intentional thermal change: top collar. Same mass, interval, lids, location and procedure.
Model panel is removable; door and roof access still work.
done: Revised cup enclosure and model with removable wall-layer panel.
Before/after sections and two control-referenced melt comparisons.
prep: Use the same equipment and interval as day 7; dry the materials before retest. Retain original data. Do not replace the experiment with a generic “improve something” task.
demo: Show the specific top-edge gap and one collar solution. Model comparing control/test pairs before making an improvement claim.
look: Check the changed feature exists and only one thermal feature changed. Ask each student to locate the collar in the section drawing.
trouble: Multiple changes made → label them; do not claim the collar alone caused the result. Roof catches insulation → move the removable panel lower and retest access.

example: Convert a checked model dimension back to full size.
7 1/2 model inches ÷ (1/2 in per ft) = 15 ft.
The result describes the intended full-size dimension, not a physically validated full-size building.
exit: At 1/2 in = 1 ft, an opening measures 1 3/4 in in the model. What real width does it represent? Identify whether opening width is read from plan, elevation, or both when dimensioned.
key: 3 1/2 ft = 3 ft 6 in. Either dimensioned view can supply width; related views must agree.
title: Inspect the Community-Room Model
product: Hand over the room model with a working door, removable roof/panel and matching drawings.
why: Construction inspection checks a list of specified features. A model can look finished while its views or opening dimensions disagree.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Completed room, top/south elevation/layer-detail drawings, person/table tokens and test records.
read: Use E for nominal room dimensions, F for the insulation detail and your revision labels for changes. Inspect the same feature across views.
measure: Each student measures the 8-in width, 6-in depth, 4-in height and door’s 1-in west offset.
Convert one actual model dimension back to feet using ÷ 1/2 in per ft; label it a represented dimension.
plan: Set up inspection table: feature | required | measured | difference | action.
Required checks: shell ±1/8 in; door width/height/offset ±1/16 in; door swing 90 degrees; roof/panel removable.
build: Exchange model and drawing set with another crew.
Inspect dimensions without changing their model. Move the person token from entrance to both tables.
Remove and replace roof and insulation panel three times each; record catches or damage.
Return inspection sheet. Owners repair one reported mismatch, or independently recheck a dimension if no fault was found.
Update drawings to match the repair. Give a one-minute demonstration of door, route and removable pieces.
Show your teacher one independent measurement and one scale conversion. Store model and test-frame together.
test: Every specified dimension has a recorded value; functional tests have explicit pass/fail.
Thermal claim cites actual cup data and does not claim a code rating or full-size building safety.
done: Inspected room model and coordinated three-view/detail set.
Each student has an individual scale, tape and plan-reading check.
prep: Prepare seven inspection sheets with the listed dimensions and pair crews. Use the same tolerances introduced during fabrication.
demo: Model an inspection entry including a failing value and an action. Show how a good drawing can document an unsuccessful experiment honestly.
look: Student locates datum and door independently. A group demonstration does not replace the individual measurement.
trouble: Drawing disagrees → identify which represents the intended requirement, then correct the other. Roof sticks → inspect tab locations before forcing it.

example: Translate a revised opening offset.
At 1/2 in per ft, changing 2 ft to 3 ft moves the opening by 1/2 in in the model.
The designer must decide the intended offset before either view is corrected.
exit: A model door must move 1 ft 6 in at scale 1/2 in = 1 ft. Calculate model movement and list the drawing views that need checking.
key: 3/4 in. Check plan and the affected wall elevation, plus any detail or parts affected by the change.
title: Clinic: Move the Door and Coordinate Both Views
product: Make a replacement south wall with the door shifted to a 3-ft west offset, then update both drawings.
why: A change order must reach every affected drawing and part. Today’s required change is precise: west offset becomes 3 ft; door size stays 3 × 7 ft.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Room model, fresh 8 × 4-in south wall, 18 in tape and spare drawing paper.
read: Original E has a 2-ft offset. Change order C-01: use 3 ft, which becomes 1 1/2 in in the model. New door edges are x=1 1/2 and 3 in.
measure: Measure and record the old door offset before removal.
Mark the new jambs and 3 1/2-in height from the same west/bottom datums on the replacement wall.
plan: Cross out the old 2-ft offset with one line on plan and south elevation; write 3 ft, C-01 and date.
Calculate model movement and mark both old and new jamb locations on a comparison sketch.
build: Cut top and right jamb of the new door; fold left jamb as before.
Remove the old south wall by peeling its tape; retain it as revision B.
Fit the new south wall with outer face flush to base. Tape to base and end walls while leaving the door free.
Move a table token only if the new door arc interferes; update that location on the plan.
Check new door offset, size, swing and token route.
Exchange views with a partner and have them locate the new opening without verbal help.
test: New left jamb is 1 1/2 in from west datum within ±1/16; opening size is unchanged.
Plan, elevation and physical wall all show C-01.
done: A physically relocated door and two coordinated revised views.
Notebook change record and original wall retained.
prep: This flex meeting uses the stated change order; no design decision is left for the teacher to invent. Have a removable sample wall joint ready.
demo: Demonstrate the 1/2-in model shift and update both views before touching the model.
look: Check students move both jambs and preserve opening width. Require one independent conversion.
trouble: Only one jamb moved → opening width changed; remake the flap. Offset measured from door flap rather than west wall end → reset the datum.

example: Use an ideal displaced-volume model.
Equal piston areas predict equal travel: A × 20 mm = A × d, so d = 20 mm.
This model fits an ideal liquid system; trapped air, leaks and friction can change actual motion.
exit: For equal piston areas, predict output travel for 18 mm input in the ideal liquid model. State why an air-filled system may behave differently and identify input/output on G.
key: 18 mm ideal output. Air is compressible; water is much less compressible under this classroom condition. Real travel must still be measured.
title: Compare Air and Water Syringe Motion
product: Operate air and water syringe pairs; attach a paper indicator and measure actual input/output travel.
why: Hydraulic technicians distinguish fluid behavior from mechanical binding. We will use measured motion, not how “strong” a system feels.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. One matching 20-mL syringe pair, 60-cm tube, water tray and towel, two 1/4 × 2-in paper pointer strips and removable tape. Teacher prepares the water fill after the air trial.
read: G labels INPUT (hand-operated) and OUTPUT (remote). Barrel stays fixed; the plunger moves. Stroke is change in plunger position, not barrel length or mL capacity.
measure: Set input to 15 mL and output to 5 mL before connecting the air-filled tube.
Tape a paper pointer to each thumb pad. Lay a ruler beside each barrel, parallel to its axis, and mark the pointer starting position.
plan: Draw input → tube → output. Label air trial pneumatic and water trial hydraulic.
Make six rows: fluid | trial | input travel mm | output travel mm | bubbles/response. Target hand stroke is 20 mm.
build: Place both syringes flat in the dry tray; partners hold BARRELS, not output plungers.
Move input forward slowly by 20 mm while partner reads output travel. Stop if resistance rises sharply; never force.
Pull input back to its original mark. Repeat three trials, swapping operator and reader.
Take the pair to the teacher for water filling at the same 15/5-mL starting positions. The tube and both tips must be water-filled, with visible bubbles removed.
Wipe outside dry. Repeat the same three 20-mm strokes and resets with water.
Check tip joints for drops and circle any delayed or unequal motion. Save the water-filled pair capped within its tray.
test: Input/output travel comes from pointer start/end positions in mm. Both students take an actual reading.
Equal-bore ideal liquid prediction is equal travel; record actual results even when they differ.
done: A working water-filled pair, clearly labeled input/output.
Six measured trial rows and a connection sketch.
prep: Prepare seven compatible pairs. Use a spare water-filled syringe to flush each tube before joining under the tray waterline. Never fit needles. Confirm each plunger has at least 20 mm safe motion from its start.
demo: Demonstrate holding a barrel while watching the moving thumb pad. Contrast milliliters on the barrel with millimeters of travel. Show the gentle stop rule.
look: Check that a student does not assist the output plunger. Air and water comparisons use matching syringes and the same stroke.
trouble: No output → check loose tube/leak and plunger sticking before retrying. Springy water trial → inspect trapped air; teacher refills. Hard stop → stop hand force and reset; do not squeeze harder.

example: Predict travel with a larger output piston.
A_in = 1 cm²; A_out = 2 cm²; input 4 cm: output = (1 × 4)/2 = 2 cm.
Ideal output force would double, but do not claim you measured a force ratio without force measurements.
exit: Input area 2 cm² moves 3 cm; output area is 3 cm². Predict output travel. Point to the mounting feature that prevents sideways motion.
key: Output = (2 × 3)/3 = 2 cm. An actual guide/brace must be identified; ideal force claims require the model’s limitations.
title: Build the Syringe-Powered Delivery Sled
product: Mount the output syringe on a card base and attach a sliding card sled that moves out and back with the hand input.
why: An actuator must be mounted so the moving part can do useful work. This device delivers a light paper load to a marked position without touching the sled.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Prepared water pair, card stock for the base, two saddle strips, one sled blank, 30 in tape and one 1 × 1-in paper cargo square. 12 × 6-in base; output nozzle at x = 3 in on centerline y = 3 in; two 4 × 1-in card saddle strips; sled blank 3 × 2 in, folded 1 in from one short end.
read: G2 is the required assembly. The syringe lies horizontally, nozzle pointing LEFT. Its plunger points RIGHT. The sled’s upright 1-in tab attaches to the output thumb pad; the 2 × 2-in deck extends to the right.
measure: Mark base datum A at lower-left; draw centerline y=3 in. Mark nozzle location x=3 in.
With output at 5 mL, check there is room to its right for the 2-in sled deck plus at least 20 mm travel before the base edge. Teacher checks fit before taping.
plan: Label base, fixed barrel, two saddle straps, moving plunger, sled tab/deck and tube on the assembly sketch.
Record two saddle locations on the smooth barrel, clear of nozzle, printed start reading and moving plunger/flange. These locations depend on the actual syringe body; measure and record them.
build: Cut base to 12 × 6 in. Cut two 4 × 1-in saddle strips and sled blank 3 × 2 in.
Fold sled across its 2-in width at 1 in from a short end. Stand the 1-in tab upright; the remaining 2 × 2-in deck lies on the base.
Lay output on centerline, nozzle at x=3 in and pointing left. Keep its 5-mL start position.
Curve each saddle over the fixed barrel, then crease its two ends down onto the base. Tape those ends firmly to the base. Do not tape or pinch the moving plunger.
Put the sled tab against the right-facing flat thumb pad, deck extending right. Tape tab to pad on both accessible sides; the deck must slide flat rather than hang above the base.
Route the 60-cm tube in a broad loop to input off the left side. Tape the tube loosely to the base near the nozzle for strain relief; never flatten the tube.
Move input slowly 20 mm. Sled should travel right. Pull input back to return the sled; do not reset it by hand.
Draw START at the sled’s front/right edge in the reset position and a delivery line 20 mm to its right. Put the paper cargo square on the deck.
test: Do three out-and-back cycles. The input hand is the only drive; output barrel stays fixed and sled clears the base edge.
Record actual sled travel each time. Classroom acceptance for equal-syringe travel is 20 mm ±2 mm, after any bubble/mount repair; failures remain recorded.
done: One water-powered sliding delivery sled with start/delivery marks and paper cargo.
Dimensioned assembly sketch and three travel readings.
prep: Preassemble a sample with the actual syringes. With nozzle at x=3 in and output at 5 mL, verify thumb pad plus 2-in deck and 20-mm travel fit a 12-in base. If the selected syringe is longer, supply a longer base and a corrected printed base dimension before release; retain all other dimensions.
demo: Show the finished moving sled, then the fixed and moving parts separately. Demonstrate saddle ends taped to the base and the upright tab attached to the thumb pad. Move only input to prove the mechanical connection.
look: Inspect each mount before water operation. Both students must locate a base coordinate and measure a stroke.
trouble: Sled tilts → refold tab 90 degrees and lower attachment so deck rests on base. Barrel creeps → tighten saddle end tape. Output jams → free plunger from saddle/tape; never force it. Bubbles → teacher reprimes.

example: Calculate an average collection rate.
180 mL in 15 s = 12 mL/s. At that average rate, 240 mL would take 20 s.
A falling reservoir changes pressure head; the reported value is the trial’s average.
exit: A system collects 200 mL in 25 s. Find average flow rate and identify two conditions to hold constant when comparing a second tube.
key: 8 mL/s. Constant starting head, liquid, tube bore when not the changed variable, collection method and timing are valid choices.
title: Measure Flow Through Two Tube Routes
product: At the prepared gravity station, time 15 mL of water through straight and curved routes; then secure a smooth tube route on the sled.
why: Pipe work requires quantities and rates as well as a route drawing. A fair comparison controls starting head, tube and outlet height.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Existing sled. Shared station: 20-mL syringe barrel with plunger removed, stand/clamp, the same 60-cm tube for both routes, catch cup, water tray, ruler and stopwatch.
read: H specifies vertical reservoir, start at 20 mL and stop at 5 mL: 15 mL passes the marks. Outlet is fixed 10 cm BELOW the 5-mL line. Compare one broad U with a broad S; no sharp kink.
measure: Measure the reservoir 5-mL-line-to-outlet vertical drop as 10 cm and secure outlet at that height.
Measure the same tube’s actual length 60 cm. Record bore only if the kit states it; do not guess from outside diameter.
plan: Sketch route A as one broad U and B as a broad S, with identical inlet/outlet locations and no uphill crest trapping air.
Make table: route | trial | volume 15 mL | time s | rate mL/s. Three trials for each route.
build: Teacher clamps the upright barrel and secures tube outlet over a cup in the tray.
Fill tube completely with water first. Pinch the tube gently near its outlet while filling reservoir above the 20-mL mark.
Release. Start the timer as the level crosses 20 mL; stop at 5 mL. Do not touch the reservoir during flow.
Refill and repeat twice. Rotate reader/timer/recorder; pairs share the recording role.
Rearrange only the middle of the tube into route B, maintaining length and both endpoint heights. Repeat three trials.
Calculate 15 ÷ time for each valid trial. A tied result is acceptable; hand timing limits small comparisons.
Reconnect the teacher-checked water pair on the sled. Route its tube in a broad untwisted loop and tape a loose guide to keep it away from the moving sled.
test: Three valid timed trials per route; same marks, tube and outlet height. Mark spills or bubbles invalid and repeat.
The sled still performs three strokes after reconnection. Gravity-flow results do not directly predict syringe-machine speed under hand pressure.
done: A secured tube route on the sled and two measured route drawings.
Six actual rates with conditions and a comparison limit.
prep: Build and rehearse the gravity station before class. If the 15-mL interval is shorter than reliable stopwatch timing, use slow-motion video timestamps at that station and teach that single timing method. Do not substitute made-up times. Run station groups while other crews inspect sled mounts.
demo: Show the start/stop meniscus crossings and fixed vertical drop. Explain why 15 mL is used even though the barrel says 20 at the start.
look: Check rates include mL/s and each crew has real station data. Do not claim U versus S must differ.
trouble: Flow stops → check air bubble, pinched tube or outlet too high. Level passes before timer ready → refill and repeat. Changed tube length → invalidate comparison and restore 60 cm.

example: Locate symmetric features from a centerline.
On a 3-in-wide hull, the centerline is 1 1/2 in from each edge. Pipes 1 in apart lie 1/2 in on each side of center.
Their centers lie 1 in and 2 in from the same edge.
exit: Two mounting centers must be 1 1/2 in apart, symmetric about the centerline of a 4-in-wide base. Find both locations from the left edge. Identify which drawing provides their spacing.
key: Centerline 2 in; offsets ±3/4 in; positions 1 1/4 and 2 3/4 in. A dimensioned plan/layout supplies spacing; schematic connectivity alone does not.
title: Add a Cargo Fence and Read the Assembly
product: Attach a three-sided cargo fence to the sled deck and make a complete measured assembly drawing.
why: Assembly drawings coordinate separate parts. You will locate a load-retaining feature without blocking actuator travel.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working sled, three 2 × 1-in card strips, one paper cargo square, 18 in tape and a dry tray.
read: G2 shows the deck 2 × 2 in. Each fence strip folds lengthwise into two 2 × 1/2-in legs. Three fences surround the front/right edge and two side edges; rear actuator tab stays accessible.
measure: Measure deck width/depth and maximum rightward travel clearance.
Mark the centerline 3 in from either long base edge. Measure barrel and saddle coordinates from the same lower-left datum.
plan: Draw the base top view and a sled side detail. Include 12 × 6 base, x=3 nozzle, y=3 axis, 2 × 2 deck and 20-mm delivery distance.
Add a parts list with two syringes, one 60-cm tube, base, two saddles, one sled and three fence strips.
build: Cut and fold the three fence strips along their centerlines.
Tape one flat leg of each strip on the deck, upright leg along each of the two sides and front/right edge. Keep tape off the underside sliding surface.
Leave the rear side open at the actuator tab. Do not bridge the moving deck to the stationary base.
Place the cargo square inside the fence. Slowly cycle out and back three times.
Measure any point where fence or tab touches a saddle. Reposition only the interfering tape/strip; do not change the delivery distance.
Exchange drawings; partner identifies all parts on the actual assembly using the labels.
test: Cargo stays on deck for three complete cycles. Fence does not bind or reduce travel.
Every listed part can be found on the drawing and object; moving and fixed parts are distinct.
done: A fenced delivery sled with a complete assembly drawing and parts list.
Notebook includes centerline/offset measurements and three cargo trials.
prep: Use the same sled for all remaining fluid lessons. No boat preparation or route choice is required. Provide one fenced sample and spare strips.
demo: Show how folding a 1-in strip creates a 1/2-in fence and attachment leg. Point to the moving/fixed boundary where tape must not cross.
look: Check actual deck dimensions and travel clearance. Ask each student to identify one symmetric location relative to the base centerline.
trouble: Sled stops early → tape likely bridges to base or catches a saddle; disconnect input motion and inspect. Fence hides joint → leave rear open so the thumb-pad connection remains visible.

example: Check a simple liquid balance.
Start 200 mL; receiver 175 mL; liquid retained 20 mL: unaccounted volume = 5 mL.
Do not call all 25 mL missing from the receiver a leak.
exit: A 150-mL trial leaves 130 mL collected and 15 mL in the route. What volume is unaccounted for? Name one check needed before calling it a leak.
key: 5 mL. Check retained liquid, spills, measurement resolution and starting/ending conditions.
title: Find and Repair a Loose Actuator Mount
product: Diagnose a deliberately loose saddle, repair it, and prove the sled repeats three accurate deliveries.
why: Repair begins with an observed fault, a predicted cause and a controlled retest. Replacing random parts can hide the original problem.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working sled, cargo square, ruler, towel and 12 in replacement tape. Teacher prepares one loose saddle end with power supplied only by hand input at rest.
read: Trace G2 from input through tube to fixed output barrel and moving sled. A moving barrel is a mounting fault; bubbles and leaks are different observations.
measure: Draw a pencil witness line at the output barrel’s original position on the base.
Measure barrel shift and sled travel during one gentle 20-mm input stroke. Stop if the mount releases.
plan: Make a fault table: symptom | suspected part | evidence | repair | retest.
Circle the suspect saddle on the assembly drawing before touching its tape.
build: Teacher peels one end of the rear saddle from the base; do not disconnect or obstruct the tube.
Operate one gentle stroke while partner watches the barrel witness line. Record the symptom.
Return input to its start; keep hands off the moving sled. Explain the suspected mount to your partner.
Remove loose tape. Reposition barrel on centerline and nozzle datum, then retape the saddle end firmly.
Dry the tray and outside connections with a towel. Inspect for fresh drops during three slow cycles; do not treat old tray water as new leakage.
Run three cargo deliveries from the same start mark and measure actual travel each time.
Add the repair and three results to the fault table.
test: Barrel stays on its witness line and each travel is 20 mm ±2 mm. Record any remaining failure.
A repair is complete only after the same motion test repeats without hands holding the output.
done: A repaired, stable sled with accessible connections.
Notebook contains symptom, evidence, a named repair and retest readings.
prep: Use only the specified loose-saddle fault. Do not make leaks or pressure blockages as surprise faults. Return input/output to their marked reset positions.
demo: Show that input motion may move an unsecured whole syringe instead of delivering useful plunger motion. Model observing first, repairing second.
look: Have students name the witness-line evidence. Independently ask one to measure output travel and one to locate the saddle on the drawing; swap next check.
trouble: Fault persists after tape repair → inspect sled drag and air separately. A dry tissue becoming wet identifies a possible joint leak; teacher disconnects/reseats and reprimes before retesting.

example: Calculate the delivery machine’s cycle rate.
5 complete cycles in 25 s = 0.20 cycles/s.
A cycle includes travel from START to DELIVERY and back to START; one outward stroke is not a cycle.
exit: A delivery machine completes 5 full cycles in 25 s. Calculate its rate in cycles/s. Name the drawing marks that define a complete cycle and cite your actual test record.
key: 0.20 cycles/s. START → 20-mm DELIVERY line → START defines one complete cycle. Actual trial data must come from the student’s notebook.
title: Time Five Delivery Cycles
product: Record three timed trials of five complete cargo-delivery cycles on the unchanged sled.
why: A baseline needs a repeatable definition. We will time the same task before and after a later mechanical change.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Sled revision A, same paper cargo, stopwatch, ruler and trial sheet.
read: G2’s START and DELIVERY lines define one cycle: sled begins at START, reaches the 20-mm line, then returns to START using input only. Five cycles make one timed trial.
measure: Verify START-to-DELIVERY separation is 20 mm; use the same sled edge at both marks.
Reset input/output and check barrel witness line before each timed trial.
plan: Make table: trial | five cycles complete? | total time s | cycles/s | faults.
Practice one untimed trial. The aim is consistent complete travel, not forceful racing.
build: Put cargo on deck. Operator holds input; timer watches the sled edge and calls “ready.”
Timer says “go” and starts clock as operator begins. Count a cycle only when sled reaches DELIVERY and returns to START.
Stop timer at the fifth return. If a cycle misses either mark, label trial invalid and record the missed endpoint.
Reset and repeat until there are three valid trials; retain invalid trials with reasons.
Rotate roles so each student operates and measures. Use gentle motion and the same cargo throughout.
Calculate 5 ÷ elapsed seconds for each trial. Calculate mean total time from the three valid trials.
Inspect the sled without modifying it. Mark the two side-fence top edges as tomorrow’s guide-rail reference.
test: Three valid five-cycle trials; every endpoint reached. No direct pushing of output.
All rates use cycles/s, not cm/s. Record observed spread rather than reporting a single fastest run.
done: Unchanged working sled revision A and a baseline timing record.
Three rates, mean time and exact cycle definition.
prep: Rehearse endpoint visibility. A short strip of contrasting tape makes the sled edge easier to see; do not change travel to make timing easier.
demo: Demonstrate one complete cycle and one incomplete cycle. Say why an outstroke alone is not a complete out-and-back cycle.
look: Watch one full trial per crew and confirm five returns. Record measuring independence separately from group performance.
trouble: Counting only outstrokes → practice slowly. Very different times → inspect missed endpoints and role changes; keep honest variation. Stiction → repair first and clearly label a new baseline after repair.

example: Compare average performance.
Speed changes from 12 to 15 cm/s: (15 − 12)/12 × 100 = 25% increase.
For time over a fixed distance, a shorter time is better; label the metric before calculating percent change.
exit: A fixed task takes 20 s before revision and 16 s after. Find percent time reduction. Explain why that is not the same numerical value as percent rate increase.
key: Time reduction 20%. For the same task, rate rises by 20/16 − 1 = 25%. Each percentage has a different baseline quantity.
title: Add Guide Rails and Retest the Sled
product: Add two fixed low guide rails beside the sled’s path, then repeat the same five-cycle timing test.
why: A controlled redesign changes one feature. Guide rails may improve alignment but can add friction; the test decides whether the change helps.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Baseline sled/data, two 3 × 1-in card strips, 18 in tape, same cargo and stopwatch.
read: G2 revision B adds two L-section rails. Fold each strip lengthwise into 1/2-in legs. Locate their vertical faces 1/8 in outside the sled’s left/right side edges across its full stroke; rails attach only to the base.
measure: At START and DELIVERY, mark the sled’s side-edge positions on the base.
Offset each guide face 1/8 in outward from the widest side position. Start each 3-in rail level with the actuator-side deck edge at START; its length covers the 2-in deck plus 20-mm stroke.
plan: Draw both rails on revision B top view; keep revision A visible. Label 1/8-in side clearance.
Copy baseline mean time; prepare three new trials using the identical five-cycle definition.
build: Cut/fold both rails into L sections.
Tape horizontal legs to the base outside the moving path; vertical legs face the sled sides. Keep tape edges off the sliding deck.
Move input slowly through the full stroke and return. The deck must not be pinched at either endpoint.
If a rail rubs, move that rail outward just enough to restore at least 1/8-in clearance; record its final location.
Run three valid five-cycle trials using the same cargo, endpoint marks and timing method as day 6.
Calculate mean time and percent time change relative to baseline. Record any cargo escape or missed endpoint separately.
Keep rails if they improve control without harmful binding. If worse, peel them off, restore revision A and record the rejected design.
test: Only guide-rail configuration changes intentionally; load, travel and cycle count stay fixed.
Do not report improvement from an incomplete or faster-but-missed delivery. A worse result is usable engineering evidence.
done: A tested rail revision, retained or removed with an evidence-based reason.
Before/after times, clearances, rates and annotated revision drawing.
