prep: Precheck rail clearance with the actual sled. Student choice is limited to retain/reject after the fixed baseline modification; this is not a new unspecified machine.
demo: Show where fixed rail tape goes and where it must not bridge to the sled. Model percent time reduction using the original baseline denominator.
look: Ask students to distinguish a 20% time reduction from a 25% rate increase for a 20-to-16-second example. Both require a fixed task.
trouble: New rail slows motion → inspect rubbing and record the tradeoff. No meaningful change → retain the data and explain the tie; do not optimize numbers by dropping valid trials.

example: Check whether a test meets its stated requirement.
A gate must move at least 20 mm. Three trials of 22, 21 and 19 mm include one failure.
An average above 20 mm does not prove every trial meets an every-cycle requirement.
exit: A 20-mm minimum travel requirement gives trials 20, 23 and 18 mm. Does the machine meet an every-cycle requirement? Calculate the mean and explain its limitation.
key: No: the 18-mm trial fails. Mean = 61/3 ≈20.3 mm; averaging conceals the failed cycle.
title: Demonstrate the Delivery Machine
product: Hand over a working syringe sled and explain its motion, measured travel and tested revision.
why: A machine handover needs operating instructions, repeatability evidence and clear limits. An average alone cannot certify every delivery.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Final sled, baseline/revision records, assembly drawing and same paper cargo.
read: Final G2 drawing must label fixed barrel, moving plunger/sled, input/output, tube and retained rails. Circle the feature that changed.
measure: Individually measure one actual 20-mm delivery stroke and the nozzle’s x position from datum A.
Review each measured travel; flag a stroke outside 20 ±2 mm even if the mean looks acceptable.
plan: Prepare a four-line operator card: load cargo; reset to START; move input until DELIVERY; pull input back to START. Add “stop if resistance rises.”
Choose one baseline and one revision result from actual notebook records, with units.
build: Exchange machines and operator cards. New operator follows the card without coaching.
Perform three complete deliveries, recording each travel and any unclear instruction.
Return the machine. Owners fix one instruction or physical snag and repeat three deliveries.
Give a one-minute demonstration identifying how input motion travels through water to the output.
Each student reads a supplied assembly location, takes a tape/ruler reading and explains one rate calculation to the teacher.
Return plungers to reset marks and store connected pair in a tray; teacher drains/stores water systems according to the kit routine after the project.
test: All three deliveries meet the classroom stroke check or remaining faults are named.
Claim only what was tested: a low-load water-powered sled, not a heated boat or measured force multiplier.
done: A working delivery machine, operator card and accurate final assembly plan.
Individual math, measurement and plan-reading evidence plus the recorded redesign.
prep: Prepare the individual-check roster and pair crews. Do not add a live pressure/load challenge during handover.
demo: Model identifying one real revised feature and citing its actual test record. Show why one failing stroke cannot be hidden by a mean.
look: Look for a new operator who can complete the task from the card, plus each student’s independent measurement.
trouble: New operator confused → improve the exact step or label, then repeat. Sled fails → record and diagnose before claiming handover complete.

example: Convert units before comparing readings.
2.4 cm = 24 mm; 24 − 20 = 4 mm above a 20-mm target.
Subtracting 2.4 from 20 without converting units gives a meaningless comparison.
exit: A drawing calls for 30 mm travel and you measure 2.7 cm. Find the shortfall and identify the start/end references to recheck.
key: 2.7 cm = 27 mm; shortfall 3 mm. Start and end must refer to the same moving point and reset position.
title: Clinic: Restore a Shifted Sled Mount
product: Locate a 5-mm mounting error, restore the supplied assembly and repeat measured travel.
why: Fault finding combines reference locations with motion measurements. The intended fault today is a shifted barrel, not a mystery chosen during class.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working sled, ruler with mm, 12 in tape and original assembly drawing.
read: G2 requires nozzle x=3 in, centerline y=3 in. Teacher shifts the fixed output barrel 5 mm sideways after loosening its saddles, leaving tube connected and unblocked.
measure: Measure actual nozzle x/y and compare to the original witness line before motion.
Convert measured 5-mm shift to cm; keep location errors separate from stroke readings.
plan: Write symptom prediction: a sideways shift can skew the tab and make the sled rub.
Mark original and shifted axes on a small plan-view sketch.
build: Inspect the deliberately shifted mount without operating it forcefully.
Explain which dimension disagrees with the plan. Partner checks the datum, not the answer.
Loosen saddle tape, restore nozzle and barrel to their original marks, then retape.
Check sled tab square to deck and clear of any retained guide rails.
Run three gentle 20-mm input strokes; record output travel and mount position each time.
Each student repeats one location measurement and one stroke measurement without partner help.
test: Nozzle returns to marked x/y location within ±2 mm; output barrel remains fixed.
Three strokes recorded; missed travel triggers inspection of bubbles/drag rather than more force.
done: A corrected mount and individual location/travel checks.
Fault → measurement → correction → retest record.
prep: Prepare exactly the stated 5-mm side shift on each machine while at rest. Do not detach tubing or damage parts. This defined flex lesson can be used for extra measurement practice.
demo: Show location and travel as two different measurements with different references. Rehearse 2.7 cm = 27 mm.
look: Students name the original datum and retain first readings. Each performs a fresh check after repair.
trouble: Stroke still short → check fluid/start position after geometry is restored. Reading from the edge of a rail instead of the base datum → reset reference.

example: Estimate wire with a stated routing allowance.
A 14-in route plus 2 in for connections needs 16 in.
Allowance is stated for this kit and layout; it is not a universal wiring rule.
exit: Three routes are 8, 11 and 6 in. Each needs a supplied 2-in connection allowance. Calculate total wire. Identify the switch symbol in J.
key: 8+11+6+3×2 = 31 in. Switch interrupts or completes a path; merely drawing a line across it does not establish physical contact.
title: Build a Door-Open Light Signal
product: Make a card door that holds a clothespin switch open when shut; opening the door pulls out a card tongue and lights one 3-V lamp.
why: A control turns a physical event into an electrical signal. The door must operate the switch; a student’s hidden finger is not the detector.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. 3-V two-AA switched holder, one 3-V lamp/holder, three alligator leads, one wooden spring clothespin, two 1 × 2-in foil strips, base 10 × 8 in, fixed wall 4 × 4 in, door 3 × 4 in, 1 × 3-in thin-card tongue and 24 in tape.
read: J1 shows the only circuit: supply + → foil jaw A; foil jaw B → lamp A; lamp B → supply −. Foil surfaces touch when the tongue is withdrawn. A closed card door inserts the insulating tongue between them.
measure: On the 10 × 8 base use the front-left corner as (0,0). Mark wall line y=3 in and hinge point (4,3). Mark tongue strip 1 × 3 in and fold 1 in from a short end.
Measure actual lead routes with a string along bends; record each run and 2-in classroom connection allowance separately from available lead length.
plan: Copy J1’s three connections with terminal labels. Trace the entire loop before attaching battery leads.
Sketch door shut/tongue inserted (lamp off) and door open/tongue out (lamp on).
build: Tape the 4 × 4-in fixed wall upright along y=3 in, from x=0 to x=4; brace it with two small folded scrap triangles cut from a 2 × 2-in square.
Tape the 3 × 4-in door to the wall’s right vertical edge. Shut, it runs from x=4 to x=7 along y=3. It opens toward the FRONT of the base (smaller y).
Wrap one foil strip over the inside face of each clothespin jaw and around the outside for a clip contact. Tape foil backs securely; keep the two foil strips separate except at the jaw contact.

Glue is not required: put clothespin BEHIND the shut door, with jaws near (6 1/2,4 1/2) and handle extending toward the rear edge. Jaws face toward the door. Tape the lower handle to the base, keeping spring/upper handle free.

Fold the tongue 90 degrees at its 1-in mark. Tape the 1-in leg vertically to the BACK of the door near its free edge, center x=6 1/2, with the fold at base level. The 2-in leg projects BEHIND the shut door toward increasing y and enters the jaws. Opening the door toward the front withdraws it. Adjust jaw position slightly for an easy sliding fit.
With holder switched OFF, clip the three leads exactly as J1’s table states. Keep exposed clips apart except at intended terminals.
Teacher checks the loop. Turn holder ON. Tongue inserted should separate foil and turn lamp off; swinging door open should withdraw tongue so jaws close and lamp turns on.
Reset by gently opening the clothespin and reinserting tongue while closing the door. The opening action must trigger automatically; manual reset is allowed and stated.
test: Open and reset the door five times. Record lamp OFF when shut and ON when opened in every trial.
Power OFF after the test. If battery or wire feels warm, switch off immediately and have teacher inspect the wiring.
done: One working card-door/clothespin light detector with labeled terminals.
Schematic, route lengths and five OFF/ON test rows.
prep: Prebuild the detector with actual clothespins and leads. Prepare seven matched kits and a completed model. Use foil jaw contacts and the specified filament lamp; no buzzer or bare-LED substitution is part of this recipe.
demo: Show the finished door action first. Explain that the card tongue is an insulator separating two conductors. Build the three-link circuit visibly with holder OFF, then demonstrate the teacher connection check.
look: Look for automatic opening-trigger and explicit manual reset. Each student traces all three connections and measures one route.
trouble: Always on → foil contacts touch around the tongue or leads bypass switch. Always off → foil faces not touching or lamp contact loose. Door buckles tongue → move clothespin rather than forcing the hinge.

example: Calculate reliability from repeated trials.
Eight successful triggers in ten trials = 80%; ten in ten = 100% in that test.
Ten successes do not prove permanent reliability under all conditions.
exit: Nine of twelve trials succeed. Calculate success percentage. Explain why moving a symbol on a schematic need not mean moving the physical component.
key: 75%. A schematic represents connectivity; physical positions are given by the layout drawing.
title: Make the Door Trigger Reliable
product: Improve the same detector with a tongue guide and verify ten repeatable door-open signals.
why: Reliability is repeatable operation under a stated procedure. You will fix alignment and distinguish circuit connectivity from physical placement.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Detector, one 3 × 1-in card strip, 12 in tape and the existing 1 × 3-in tongue.
read: J1 schematic is unchanged. Add a loose paper guide loop around the tongue just before the clothespin jaws; it guides the tongue but must not contact foil electrically.
measure: Measure tongue travel needed to fully clear the foil jaws. Mark that point with pencil.
Measure the clothespin jaw location from base datum and add it to the physical layout.
plan: Draw a separate schematic and base layout. The schematic shows connections; the layout shows actual component locations.
Make a ten-row table: tongue inserted OFF | door open ON | reset success.
build: Switch holder OFF. Wrap the 3 × 1-in strip loosely around the tongue to make a sleeve; leave about 1/16 in sliding clearance.
Tape the sleeve ends to the fixed base/wall beside the clothespin, keeping it clear of jaws and foil.
Slide tongue through the sleeve into the open clothespin, then release jaws and close door.
Teacher checks connections remain unchanged. Turn holder ON and perform ten door-open/manual-reset cycles.
Swap operator after five. Record each state, not only an overall percentage.
If it catches, widen the sleeve or realign clothespin once. Repeat the full ten cycles and label the revision.
Power OFF and label final jaw/guide locations on the layout.
test: Target ten correct OFF/ON pairs with no hidden contact assistance; record any failure.
Moving the clothespin changes layout coordinates but need not change the schematic connections.
done: A detector with guided tongue and two distinct drawings.
Ten-trial reliability record before/after any adjustment.
prep: Have spare tongue strips if creased. Show the loose guide and a deliberately overtight sample as a contrast during the demo.
demo: Demonstrate the same circuit with the lamp moved elsewhere on the base. Explain why its schematic connections are unchanged.
look: Check ten actual cycles and both lamp states. Ask each student to locate a part on the layout and trace its connection on the schematic.
trouble: Tongue jams → open the guide clearance and align it with jaws. Lamp flickers open → clean/flatten foil contact and inspect clips with power OFF.

example: Compare a reading with a nominal value.
A nominal 3.0-V source reads 2.8 V: difference = −0.2 V.
A nominal rating is not a guaranteed measurement; interpret readings with the circuit condition and instrument resolution.
exit: A nominal 4.5-V source reads 4.2 V. Find the difference. On the schematic identify two points for measuring lamp voltage and state the required measurement mode.
key: −0.3 V relative to nominal. Across the lamp terminals in the taught DC-voltage mode. Teacher verifies instrument-specific sockets/range.
title: Measure Voltage Across the Source and Lamp
product: At the teacher meter station, measure DC voltage across source and lamp, then diagnose one opened lamp connection.
why: Voltage is a difference between two points. Correct probe placement helps trace an open path without guessing or rewiring randomly.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working detector; supervised digital multimeter with black lead in COM and red in V input; the demonstrated DC-voltage range above 3 V (typically 20 V on a manual-range meter).
read: J marks source +/− and lamp A/B. For source voltage probe + and −; for lamp voltage probe A and B. Use the teacher’s labeled DC-V setup; do not move leads to current sockets.
measure: Observe teacher confirm COM/V sockets, DC-V mode and suitable range on the actual meter.
Record source and lamp readings with tongue out (lamp on) and tongue inserted (lamp off); label both state and volts.
plan: Draw a voltmeter circle across source terminals, then a second example across lamp terminals. It bridges two test points; it is not inserted by removing a wire.
Prepare table: circuit condition | two test points | reading V | observation.
build: Switch holder OFF while placing clips safely. Teacher checks that probes cannot bridge adjacent terminals.
Turn ON. Hold insulated probe handles and take the demonstrated source reading, then lamp A-to-B reading with tongue out.
Insert tongue and repeat lamp reading in OFF state. Do not infer every unseen circuit condition from this single reading.
Power OFF. Teacher removes the lead from lamp terminal A and parks the loose clip away from other conductors.
Power ON under supervision. Note lamp off; measure source then lamp using the same test points.
Power OFF, identify the disconnected terminal by tracing J, reconnect it and repeat the working lamp reading.
Return probes to station and store detector with holder OFF.
test: Teacher directly observes each student’s correct DC-V mode and across-two-points connection.
Working source remains available during the open-lamp fault; actual readings depend on meter resolution and contact. No readings are invented when a station turn is pending.
done: A restored working detector.
Actual state-labeled source/lamp voltage readings and identified open connection.
prep: Set one protected teacher station and label the actual sockets/range using the meter manual. All crews continue detector layout/ten-cycle checks while awaiting a scheduled turn. The only fault is the removed lamp-A lead.
demo: Demonstrate across versus in-series using unplugged leads. State that a meter setting must be checked before touching a live test point.
look: Record each student’s direct measurement separately. Readings need units and state; a bare number is insufficient.
trouble: Negative reading → check probe polarity and explain the sign. No stable value → inspect probe contact and range. Never try a current mode to solve an uncertain voltage reading.

example: Use Ohm’s law for an explicitly resistive example.
For a 30-ohm resistor at 3.0 V, I = V/R = 0.10 A = 100 mA.
Do not assume a motor, lamp or LED behaves like a constant resistor across all conditions.
exit: A supplied 60-ohm resistor is connected to 3.0 V. Calculate current in A and mA. Show where a current meter enters the series path.
key: 0.05 A = 50 mA. It replaces a break in the series path using the demonstrated setup, never bridges the source.
title: Measure Current in the Lamp Branch
product: At the supervised station, insert the meter into one break in the lamp circuit, record current, then restore the detector.
why: Current measurement requires the circuit’s charge flow to pass through the instrument. This is a different connection from voltage measurement.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Detector and teacher-operated meter station: fused current input/range suitable for the kit lamp rating, insulated leads and meter manual. Teacher makes and approves all current-mode wiring.
read: J shows the break between switch output and lamp A. The current meter replaces that one connection in series. It never bridges supply + and −.
measure: Teacher states the lamp rated current and the chosen meter input/range before the measurement.
Each student reads the stable current display with unit; teacher confirms A or mA and records the circuit condition.
plan: Draw the series insertion at the switch-to-lamp break. Draw the original direct lead beside it for restoration.
Work the supplied resistor example as a MODEL exercise; the filament lamp is not a constant 30-ohm resistor.
build: Switch holder OFF and remove the original switch-to-lamp lead.
Teacher connects switch output to the meter current input and meter COM to lamp A, using the actual instrument’s fused rated input.
Teacher inspects the complete loop and selected current range, then permits holder ON with tongue out.
Each student reads and records current. Turn holder OFF before touching any wiring.
Teacher removes meter and restores the original switch-to-lamp lead. Return red meter lead to its V socket for storage.
Run three detector OFF/ON cycles to confirm restoration.
Compare the measured current with the stated lamp rating as an observation; do not force an Ohm-law match using an invented resistance.
test: Every current reading includes unit and supervised series connection. No student experiments with meter sockets under power.
Detector works after meter removal; original loop is fully restored.
done: Restored detector and an independently read current measurement.
Series-insertion sketch, A/mA conversion and separate supplied-resistor calculation.
prep: Confirm meter fuse and current rating with the manual; use only a rated low-voltage lamp circuit. Teacher controls setup and wiring changes at one station. If suitable meter is absent, this lesson remains pending while students complete a defined detector reliability/diagram practice; it is not signed off.
demo: Show how removing one wire creates two points for a SERIES insertion. Contrast with yesterday’s voltage probes across the lamp.
look: Observe each student identify series location and read units. Do not award hands-on measurement from a worksheet alone.
trouble: Unexpected zero → power OFF and inspect the open series loop/fuse using the manual. Never move to a larger source or bypass the fuse. Incorrect reading units → inspect display annunciator before converting.

example: List every control state.
Two independent on/off switches give 2 × 2 = 4 states: off/off, on/off, off/on, on/on.
Testing only both-on does not establish independent control.
exit: List the four states and expected lamp outputs for two independent switches. If one 9-in route needs 2 in allowance, how long is that wire?
key: 00 neither; 10 first only; 01 second only; 11 both. Wire length 11 in. Match bit order to the labeled switch/lamp pair.
title: Wire Two Independently Lit Rooms
product: Build a two-room card model on an 8 × 6-in base; wire each 3-V lamp through its own switch in parallel.
why: Independent controls require independent branches sharing a source. Testing all four switch states proves more than simply lighting both lamps.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. 3-V holder, two 3-V lamps/holders, two SPST switches, eight alligator leads, base 8 × 6 in, two outer walls 8 × 3 in, three wall blanks 6 × 3 in and 36 in tape. Retain door detector separately for next lesson.
read: J connection table: +→S1-1→S1-2→L1-A→L1-B→−; second branch +→S2-1→S2-2→L2-A→L2-B→−. Each arrow between components is a lead; the switch and lamp each have two terminals.
measure: Mark base center divider x=4 in from left datum. Mark lamp centers (2,3) and (6,3) in.
Mark S1 at (2,1) and S2 at (6,1). Measure actual lead routes; no cutting commercial leads.
plan: Copy both branches with labels. Make state table S1/S2: OFF/OFF, ON/OFF, OFF/ON, ON/ON.
Draw physical layout with the specified centers and battery just outside the rear wall.
build: Cut base and wall blanks. Tape 8 × 3-in front/rear walls upright on the base.
Dry-fit and trim left/right/divider 6 × 3-in blanks to the gap between front/rear walls. Tape outside walls at base edges and divider centered on x=4.
Tape lamp holders and switches at their marked positions. Keep terminals accessible; route leads over the open wall tops.
Holder OFF: connect + to S1-1, S1-2 to L1-A, L1-B to −. These are the first branch’s three leads.
Connect + to S2-1, S2-2 to L2-A, L2-B to − with three more leads. Share the marked supply terminals without letting + clips touch − clips.
Teacher checks branches and combined lamp rating. Turn holder ON and test all four states in order.
Correct any misconnection with holder OFF; repeat all four states. Label rooms 1/2 and lamps L1/L2.
test: 00: neither lamp; 10: L1 only; 01: L2 only; 11: both. Repeat the four-state sequence three times.
Changing one switch must not change the other lamp. Record all twelve checks.
done: Two-room model with independently controlled lamps and accessible wiring.
Matched schematic/layout and twelve state-test results.
prep: Check the two-lamp load against battery holder/switch ratings using kit information. Provide spare leads. The model is open-top and has no need for mains wiring.
demo: Build one branch, then trace the second from the same + to the same −. Demonstrate that placing S2 in a shared return would break independence.
look: Have each student trace and measure one branch. Verify four states rather than accepting a photograph of both lamps on.
trouble: Both follow one switch → switch sits in a shared segment; restore separate branches. One never lights → power OFF and trace its three leads/holder contacts. Warm supply → OFF immediately and teacher checks for a bypass short.

example: Calculate power for a supplied steady operating point.
A motor’s startup and changing-load behavior may differ from this steady example.
exit: A supplied steady device operates at 4.5 V and 0.10 A. Calculate power. Explain why that single value is not automatically its startup power.
key: 0.45 W. Startup/load conditions may change current; distinguish the supplied steady point from actual operation.
title: Add the Door Signal to Room Two
product: Replace room 2’s manual switch with the clothespin door detector; room 1 remains independently switched.
why: A useful control responds to a condition. We will make room 2’s light act as a door-open signal without changing room 1.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two-room model, retained clothespin/foil switch, one 3 × 3-in card door, 1 × 3-in tongue, guide strip and 18 in tape. No added electrical load is required.
read: Required revised branch: +→clothespin jaw A; jaw B→L2-A; L2-B→−. Room 1’s S1/L1 branch is unchanged. S2 is removed and stored, not left ambiguously in series.
measure: Mark a 2 1/2 × 2 1/2-in door opening in room 2’s front wall, right jamb 1/2 in from the right outside corner; mark the left jamb 2 1/2 in farther toward the center divider.
Measure tongue travel and locate the clothespin INSIDE room 2 so a shut door inserts a tongue pointing into the room; keep clips accessible from the open top.
plan: Draw the new room 2 schematic with detector contacts replacing S2. Cross out S2 on the revision, not on the original record.
State table is now S1 OFF/ON × door SHUT/OPEN; predict all four outputs.
build: Power OFF and remove room 2’s two switch leads from S2.
Cut the door opening out of room 2’s front wall; preserve the surrounding wall. Tape a 3 × 3-in door over it along the left jamb to form an outward-opening hinge.

Fold the 1 × 3-in tongue 1 in from a short end. Tape the 1-in leg vertically INSIDE the lower free edge of the door, fold at base level, so its 2-in leg points into room 2. Put clothespin inside the room with jaws facing the front wall and handle toward the rear. Shut door inserts tongue; outward opening withdraws it.
Attach a loose guide loop just before the jaws, using the earlier detector method.
Connect supply + to jaw A and jaw B to L2-A; keep L2-B return to −. Remove unused S2 from the model.
Teacher checks circuit. Power ON and test four states: S1 off/door shut, S1 on/shut, S1 off/open, S1 on/open.
Repeat each state three times. Reset the door by opening clothespin to reinsert tongue. Power OFF for storage.
test: L1 follows only S1; L2 follows door position (shut OFF, open ON). All twelve state checks recorded.
Door opens without snagging wires; reset method is printed on the model.
done: A two-room model with room 1 light switch and room 2 door-open signal.
Revised schematic, layout and four-state table.
prep: Precheck cut opening fits the model’s actual room-2 width. This extension reuses the existing lamp and detector; no fan, buzzer or additional choice is required.
demo: Show exactly which two S2 leads move to the two foil contacts. Point out that the detector replaces a switch, not a lamp or return path.
look: Observe independence and automatic door-open trigger. Each student identifies the changed branch on the schematic.
trouble: Room 1 changes with door → detector accidentally installed in shared supply/return; restore J branch separation. Tongue snags → guide alignment, not electrical rewiring, is the needed repair.

example: Calculate energy and sample operating cost.
Two 0.30-W lights for 4 h: 2 × 0.30 × 4 = 2.4 Wh = 0.0024 kWh. At a supplied $0.25/kWh, cost is $0.0006.
Sample electricity price is not a current tariff. Energy cost does not include battery purchase or equipment cost.
exit: A 0.6-W fan runs for 3 h. Find Wh and kWh. At a supplied $0.20/kWh, find energy cost and state one expense excluded.
key: 1.8 Wh = 0.0018 kWh; $0.00036. Excludes batteries, device purchase and other costs. Small model power legitimately gives a small energy-only amount.
title: Make an Operating Schedule and Energy Estimate
product: Use the actual model to demonstrate two room-use schedules, then calculate their energy with supplied lamp-power values.
why: Energy depends on both power and time. A useful schedule keeps necessary functions while avoiding unnecessary run time.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working model, timer, two 3 × 5-in schedule cards and notebook. Use supplied calculation value 0.30 W per lamp; label it ASSUMED, not measured.
read: K: power W × time h = energy Wh; divide Wh by 1,000 for kWh. Keep each branch’s operating interval separate.
measure: Demonstrate schedule A for 60 seconds: S1 on and door open throughout; both lamps on.
Demonstrate schedule B for 60 seconds: S1 on throughout; door open for the first 15 seconds, then shut. Record actual state timings.
plan: Calculation schedule A represents both lamps on for 4 h. B represents L1 on 4 h and L2 on 1 h. The classroom minute is a compressed demonstration, not four hours of measured energy.
Calculate both using the supplied 0.30-W value and compare Wh.
build: Write schedule A and B on separate cards with all switch/door instructions.
Run A, then power OFF while preparing the reset. Run B and have another crew observe the changing lamp states.
Calculate A: 2 × 0.30 × 4. Calculate B: 0.30 × 4 + 0.30 × 1.
Find saved Wh and percent reduction relative to A. Calculate sample energy-only cost at $0.25/kWh.
Attach schedule B beside the control and demonstrate it once more to a new operator.
Store the model with holder OFF; do not leave it running for the imagined four-hour schedule.
test: Model demonstrates the stated switching sequence; calculations explicitly use assumed 0.30 W and represented hours.
Energy cost is not battery purchase cost or a battery-runtime prediction.
done: A model with a usable schedule card and verified state sequence.
Two energy budgets, saved Wh and labeled assumptions.
prep: Use supplied values for every crew so equipment variation does not disguise the arithmetic. No generator kit is needed. Keep actual observed seconds separate from represented hours.
demo: Model one branch calculation and explain why watts and watt-hours differ. Show A=2.4 Wh, B=1.5 Wh, saving0.9 Wh (37.5%).
look: Look for both branches in the budget and kWh conversion before multiplying by the sample tariff. Each student calculates independently.
trouble: Student uses 60 seconds as 60 hours → separate demonstration column from calculation schedule. Cost too large → check Wh-to-kWh division by 1,000.

example: Check a reliability claim.
Four required switch states × three repeats = 12 checks. Eleven passes means one condition still needs repair.
Do not hide a failed control state inside an overall average.
exit: Two switch states are tested three times each and one fails twice. How many checks passed? Explain what the failed state tells an inspector to investigate.
key: 6 total checks, 4 passed. Investigate the branch/trigger/connections associated with that state; percentage alone does not locate the fault.
title: Find an Open Return and Hand Over the Controls
product: Diagnose a removed L2 return lead, repair it, and repeat all four control states before handover.
why: A specific symptom should lead to a specific branch check. The final handover proves both the repaired function and unaffected function still work.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Final model, revised schematic, twelve-check sheet and existing leads. Teacher removes L2-B return at the lamp while holder is OFF and parks the clip safely.
read: Use the final schematic: S1 controls L1; detector controls L2. The selected fault is an OPEN L2 return, not a short or an unspecified hidden defect.
measure: Inspect all actual connection points against the revised schematic and label the disconnected terminal.
Measure one route from component to supply along its actual bends; add the supplied 2-in planning allowance.
plan: Predict outputs for all four S1/door states with the open L2 return.
Write diagnosis before repair: which branch cannot complete a path and which should still function.
build: Teacher prepares the one stated open connection with power OFF.
Power ON briefly and observe four states; record symptoms without moving clips.
Power OFF. Trace L2’s entire path and point to the missing return link on the drawing.
Reconnect L2-B to supply −; teacher checks exposed clips are separated.
Power ON and repeat all four S1/door states three times. Record each of twelve checks.
Give a one-minute handover with door-reset and power-off instructions. Each student performs an individual schematic/measurement/math check.
Power OFF and inventory lamps, switches, leads and cells.
test: L1 remains independent and L2 responds to door after repair; all twelve checks documented.
Fault report names the open return and evidence rather than “the battery was bad” without a test.
done: A working, inspected control model and short operator note.
Individual check record plus fault/repair/retest evidence.
prep: Prepare only the specified L2-B open fault. Use no current-meter faults or deliberate shorts. Keep old manual S2 labeled in the kit.
demo: Trace one complete branch aloud, then model predicting which output is affected by an open return.
look: Record measuring, plan reading and math separately. A student who did not independently demonstrate a skill remains not observed and gets a focused retry.
trouble: Both lamps off → inspect shared source switch/connections, not the intended single-branch fault. Repair fixes one state only → repeat full table and inspect trigger geometry.

example: Find an offset from a dimension chain.
Overall run 12 in; first segment 3 1/4 in; last segment 2 1/2 in: middle = 6 1/4 in.
All three lengths must refer to consecutive segments on the same route.
exit: A 15-in route contains 4 3/4-in and 3 1/2-in end segments. Find the middle segment and name the drawing needed to measure physical routing.
key: 6 3/4 in. Use the dimensioned physical layout; a schematic alone does not specify route lengths.
title: Clinic: Lay Out Mounting Centers and Trace a Branch
product: Make the four-center paper template and use it to explain physical location versus electrical connection.
why: Installers need both a layout and a schematic. One locates a component; the other tells what connects to it.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. One 8 1/2 × 5 1/4-in paper sheet per student, completed model and final schematic. No drilling.
read: C’s four centers are 3/4 in from adjacent edges. Label them P1–P4 clockwise starting lower-left. They are paper mounting references, not new live connection points.
measure: Individually mark x=3/4 and 7 3/4; y=3/4 and 4 1/2 in from lower-left datum.
Check one actual model component’s x/y location and one routed lead length.
plan: Draw light coordinate guides and mark four crosses. Copy actual component coordinates to the model layout.
Trace the room-2 electrical path in a different notebook sketch using terminal names.
build: Cut the paper outline and mark all four centers without teammate assistance.
Exchange and inspect offsets within ±1/16 in; retain corrections beside original marks.
Put template beside the actual model, not on live terminals. Explain which measurement method transfers to component placement.
Power OFF and trace room 2 from supply + through detector/lamp to −. Read each terminal label aloud.
Replace one worn layout label and retest the four states after teacher check.
Complete a fresh independent route subtraction and show the teacher one center measurement.
test: Four located centers meet the paper tolerance; model layout has actual coordinates.
Student chooses layout for position and schematic for connectivity.
done: An individual mounting template and corrected model documentation.
Separate physical-location and circuit-path explanations.
prep: Use this defined flex lesson for measurement/plan practice. Prepare a large C drawing and model with intact wiring; no new surprise fault is needed.
demo: Ask “Where is it?” with the layout, then “What connects to it?” with the schematic; demonstrate one of each.
look: Each student performs their own center mark and branch trace. Do not accept a partner’s completed template.
trouble: Schematic used to measure wire length → use actual physical route. Mixed inch/mm coordinates → relabel and convert before comparison.

example: Explain a defensible performance comparison.
A task improves from 30 s to 24 s: time reduction = 6/30 × 100 = 20%.
Choose a metric meaningful to your product and preserve the original procedure.
exit: Using your own project, show a calculation with units and identify its baseline or reference. Interpret one supplied-plan feature and cite the notebook page containing its physical check.
key: Open response: verify operation, units, baseline/reference, drawing interpretation and actual check independently. Accept unsuccessful tests with a sound diagnosis; do not invent a numerical key.
title: Prepare the Working Controls Exhibition
product: Prepare the completed two-room control model for a two-minute demonstration with one drawing and one real test record.
why: A vocational demonstration must show a function and explain evidence. Today’s required exhibit is the control model, so every crew knows what to prepare.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Final two-room model, final schematic/layout, state-test and repair records, one 3 × 5-in operator card and 12 in repair tape.
read: Use the final control schematic with the door detector replacing S2. Keep the physical layout beside it and circle the actual repair/revision.
measure: Individually remeasure one component location or lead route using its original datum.
Repeat all four S1/door states and record actual outputs before preparing the demonstration.
plan: Write a two-minute sequence: 20 s purpose; 40 s four states; 30 s drawing/measurement; 30 s repair and evidence.
Choose one real calculation from your notebook with given values, units and result; prepare to explain it without a teammate.
build: A new partner operates the model using only its card. Mark any unclear instruction or snag.
Power OFF before repair. Fix that one physical issue or rewrite the exact unclear instruction; if none was found, improve a missing terminal label.
Repeat all four states after the change.
Put model, schematic, layout and one test record on the table. A slideshow is not required.
Rehearse the two-minute sequence. Each student operates and explains one distinct skill; trio roles rotate.
Label setup/reset/power-off steps on the operator card. Store the checked exhibit with holder OFF.
test: New operator can reset door and demonstrate independent branches from the card.
Each student can show their own measured value and calculation; a decorative poster does not replace either.
done: A ready two-room control exhibit with operator card and evidence.
One corrected detail and a rehearsed demonstration.
prep: Set up seven exhibition spots with table space and identify visiting crew pairs. The required exhibit is the completed controls project; earlier projects can be displayed alongside only after this is ready.
demo: Give a two-minute model demonstration showing the object first, then one drawing and one calculation. Keep the evidence concise.
look: Check every crew has a real functioning exhibit or a clearly documented fault under repair. Observe each student’s distinct contribution.
trouble: Exhibit unreliable → use work time on the actual fault, not presentation decoration. Student reads a memorized claim → ask them to locate and remeasure the feature.

example: Apply a stated dimensional tolerance.
Target 5 1/2 in ±1/8 in gives 5 3/8 through 5 5/8 in. An actual 5 3/4 in is 1/8 in above the upper limit.
Tolerance is a stated acceptance range; function still needs testing.
exit: A supplied part is 7 1/4 in ±1/8 in. State the interval and inspect a 7 3/8-in part. Then name one vocational skill you can now demonstrate independently, with evidence.
key: 7 1/8 through 7 3/8 in, inclusive; the part meets the dimensional interval. Individual evidence must support the student’s chosen skill.
title: Demonstrate, Inspect and Complete Individual Checks
product: Run the control exhibition and complete each student’s independent trades-math, measuring and plan-reading check.
why: A finished course should show skills each person can perform. Team products provide the context; individual demonstrations establish the learning.
kit: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Prepared control exhibit, operator card, notebook and final drawings; teacher roster for four separate skill checks.
read: Use the final schematic to trace one complete branch and the layout to locate a component from the stated datum. The supplied tolerance problem is a separate inspection exercise.
measure: Each student measures one assigned component position or lead route without partner help, naming endpoints and units.
Compare measured value with the student’s final drawing and record signed difference.
plan: Mark where your notebook shows an actual repair, retest and calculation.
Read the supplied tolerance transfer problem independently; state both limits before deciding acceptance.
build: Set up exhibit with power OFF; teacher inspects connections before operation.
Demonstrate four control states to the visiting crew. Rotate operator, drawing explainer and inspector roles.
Visitor records one specific observation: correct function, unclear step or located mismatch.
Power OFF, correct that exact issue if present and repeat affected states; if none, complete the full final four-state check.
At the teacher station each student: traces one branch; measures a physical dimension; solves the tolerance calculation; explains a named repair and retest.
Record any still-missing skill as pending and complete a focused retry while other students inventory and store equipment.
Power OFF, separate cells only under the kit storage routine, count parts and submit the single individual app response.
test: All four control states demonstrated or the remaining fault precisely identified.
Teacher records math, measuring, plan interpretation and build/revision separately for every student.
done: Completed demonstration, stored kit and individual vocational-skills record.
Final notebook contains drawing, measurement, calculation and real revision evidence.
prep: Use a 15-student roster with four columns. Schedule brief individual checks throughout Make/Test, about 3 minutes each while other crews exhibit or retry. Keep the physical measurement prompt fresh for each student.
demo: Show the four things the individual check requires. Model naming a datum and units before reading the tape. Explain that a missing observation is a next check, not automatic crew credit.
look: Use independent / with cue / not observed and record the actual evidence. Offer one focused retry without supplying the answer.
trouble: Time runs out for a student → record the specific remaining check and schedule its completion; do not infer mastery. Product fails → a sound diagnosis is valid evidence but does not become a passing function test.
